CHIEF COMPLAINT
Right heel pain, worse after workouts and first thing in the morning, while training for a triathlon.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Dennis is a patient seen for the first time in this office. He is training for a triathlon and reports pain in the back of the right heel that extends up into the calf. The pain occurs typically after a workout and when he first gets up in the morning. On first getting out of bed the area feels very tight and "almost like it's tearing." It eases somewhat after walking for about 10 to 15 minutes. It becomes sore again if he sits for an extended period and then gets up, and after a lot of activity. The pain is mainly on the right; the left is not affected.

Training: he runs about 10 km in the morning, bikes 45 minutes to an hour at lunchtime, and swims 30 minutes to an hour in the evening. He trains five days a week. On weekends he alternates a long run and a long bike, and he does not do a long swim. He takes one day off. He does not stretch at all because he does not have time. On the bike he starts slowly and goes faster once warmed up. Prior treatment was not asked about, but the doctor assumed that whatever he had been doing was not working significantly.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Musculoskeletal: Right heel and posterior calf pain as per HPI. No left leg pain.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Lower extremities, right:
- Dorsiflexion of the foot and ankle causes mild pain.
- Resisted movement against the examiner's hand causes mild pain.
- Thompson test is negative. Squeezing the calf is not painful bilaterally.
- Squeezing the heel causes significant pain.
- The Achilles tendon is very tender to palpation moving up from the heel.
Left: calf squeeze not painful.

RESULTS
No imaging or laboratory results. X-ray was not felt to be needed at this point.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Achilles tendinitis, right, due to overuse from aggressive triathlon training. The Thompson test is negative.
- Stop training for 1 to 2 weeks to allow healing.
- Ibuprofen (Advil) 3 tablets every 6 hours as an anti-inflammatory.
- Order physical therapy for a couple of visits for stretching and strengthening of the lower extremities, with education on how to stretch before activity.
- No x-ray at this time.
- Follow up in 7 to 10 days, after the first couple of physical therapy appointments, to monitor progress. The office staff will schedule it.
- If he still has significant pain at about 10 days without change despite activity modification, more aggressive treatment options will be considered.
- The patient agreed with the plan.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Follow-up of chronic problems: depression, hypertension, and rotator cuff repair.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Edward is a 59-year-old male with a past medical history significant for depression, hypertension, and prior rotator cuff repair who presents for follow-up of his chronic problems. He was last seen about six months ago.

Depression: At the last visit he was considering new strategies to manage his depression and did not want to start medication because he is already on multiple medications. He reports the past six months have gone well. He sees a counselor once a week and has been swimming frequently over the summer and fall. He does not feel the need to start medication at this time and knows he can call if that changes.

Hypertension: Blood pressure was difficult to control six months ago. He reports good days and bad days. He takes his medication (Norvasc) daily. He admits occasional dietary indiscretion with burgers, wine, and salt. He checks his blood pressure about once a week at a CVS pharmacy machine.

Rotator cuff repair: Repair was done about eight months ago. He reports it is doing well. He has progressed from physical therapy to home exercises, stretching with a yoga ball once a week, and is getting stronger each time.

He also notes mild ankle swelling, mainly toward the end of the day, which resolves by the next morning.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Respiratory: Denies shortness of breath.
Cardiovascular: Denies chest pain. Reports ankle swelling at the end of the day that resolves by morning.
HEENT: Denies nasal congestion.
Psychiatric: Depression well managed per HPI.
Other systems were reviewed on the check-in sheet, and the doctor noted he appeared to be doing well.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Blood pressure 156/94. Home/pharmacy blood pressure readings have been running a little high over the past couple of months.
Cardiovascular: Slight 3/6 systolic ejection murmur, previously noted and stable.
Respiratory: Lungs clear.
Extremities: 1 to 2+ pitting edema in the legs.

RESULTS
Labs: Look good overall. Creatinine (kidney function) is stable.
EKG: Normal. No evidence of coronary artery disease.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
59-year-old male with depression, hypertension, and prior rotator cuff repair presenting for follow-up.

1. Depression: Well managed with counseling, swimming, and a good support system. No medication needed at this time. He may call if he feels he needs to start medication.

2. Hypertension: Not well controlled. Office BP is 156/94 and recent readings have been elevated. Leg edema is present, and dietary salt intake may be contributing. Plan:
- Increase Norvasc to 10 mg daily.
- Order an echocardiogram.
- Order a lipid panel.
- Discuss diet and decreasing salt intake.

3. Rotator cuff repair: Doing well and essentially resolved. Continue home exercises. No further intervention needed.

The patient had no questions.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Follow-up for diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and peripheral vascular disease.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Maria Martin, DOB 03/05/1946, presents for follow-up. She consented to recording. She feels "pretty good" overall.

Diabetes: Last A1c was 9.9. She received a letter instructing her to increase glimepiride to 4 mg twice daily but has remained on 2 mg. She just filled the prescription. Diet: no pasta, little bread (wheat bread, about two slices in the morning), occasional peanut butter sandwiches, hardly any soda, drinks club soda/seltzer. She continues metformin.

Eyes: Eye exams are up to date, and she recently got new glasses. She sees the optometry group on Liberty Road and previously saw Dr. Sanchez. She had cataract surgery and waited a month to heal before getting her prescription. She is not happy with the lens in one eye; the other is good.

Hypertension: Home BP a couple of weeks ago was 116. She reports taking metoprolol 50 mg daily, lisinopril/hydrochlorothiazide 20/25 mg daily, and amlodipine 10 mg daily.

Hyperlipidemia and vascular disease of the legs: On atorvastatin and tolerating it. She reports her feet feel "like hell" all the time, her legs bother her, and she cannot walk much. She wonders about sciatica. She also has pain up to the hips and upper legs. She is trying to walk. Symptoms are felt to be relatively stable.

Tobacco: Still smoking, not ready to quit, but will think about it.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: No fever or chills.
Eyes: Vision improved after cataract surgery, but she is unhappy with the lens in one eye.
Respiratory: Recent cough with congestion, clear sputum, improved this morning. No shortness of breath.
Cardiovascular: No chest pain, pressure, or tightness.
GI: No nausea, vomiting, or GI symptoms.
GU: Slower urinary stream, stable. Urinates several times per day. Nocturia only occasionally. Drinks fluids in the evening.
Musculoskeletal: Pain in the hips and upper legs.
Neurologic: No headaches or dizziness. Foot discomfort as above.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Neck: Carotids normal, no bruits.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm, S1 and S2 crisp, no murmurs.
Lungs: Clear, no rales or wheezing.
Extremities: No edema. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses palpable. Thickened nails. Mildly dry skin, no skin breakdown. Mildly decreased sensation at the tips of the first and second toes.
Vitals: BP recheck 140/60.

RESULTS
Prior A1c 9.9 (blood sugar average above 9). No new results today; labs drawn today.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Type 2 diabetes, uncontrolled (A1c 9.9): Increase glimepiride. Until the supply runs out, take two 2 mg tablets twice daily. A new prescription will be written for 4 mg, one tablet twice daily. Continue metformin. Monitor for hypoglycemia (weak, shaky, sweaty) and call if it occurs. Recheck labs today. Dietary advice: cut down on bread slices per day.
2. Peripheral neuropathy, mild: Keep feet moisturized. A medication is available if symptoms worsen, but she is already on many medications. She may use an over-the-counter foot cream or scrub.
3. Hypertension: Office BP 140/60, with better home readings. Continue metoprolol 50 mg daily, lisinopril/HCTZ 20/25 mg daily, and amlodipine 10 mg daily. Check kidney function today.
4. Hyperlipidemia and peripheral vascular disease: Continue high-dose atorvastatin to protect the arteries. Symptoms are relatively stable. Encourage walking.
5. Tobacco use: Advised to quit. She is not ready, but will think about it.
6. Cataract surgery, status post: She is unhappy with one lens. Laser cleanup may be an option, and she should follow up with her eye doctor.
7. Follow-up: Labs today. Return in four months. Continue everything else unchanged.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Follow-up after an emergency room visit for shortness of breath.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Louis is a 58-year-old male with a history of congestive heart failure who presents for follow-up after an emergency room visit. On Saturday he was playing tennis in very hot, humid weather. After about half an hour he became very short of breath and struggled to breathe. He feared he was having a heart attack, and his wife took him to the ER, where everything checked out. About six hours after returning home, he felt lightheaded and very dizzy. On Sunday he felt fine. He sought follow-up to be checked.

He reports taking all of his heart failure medications diligently and is in touch with his doctor. He tries to avoid salt and junk food but admits to cheating every now and then.

He had a cataract removed from his eye three months ago, and he reports no vision problems since. He had a skin cancer removed about five months ago, which healed nicely without problems.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Felt fine on Sunday after the episode.
Eyes: No vision problems.
Respiratory: Shortness of breath with exertion in the heat on Saturday, as per HPI.
Neurological: Lightheadedness and dizziness about six hours after returning home from the ER, resolved by Sunday.
Skin: No problems at the skin cancer excision site.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Blood pressure is a little high. The ER report also noted high blood pressure.
Neck: Very supple. No jugular venous distention.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm, no murmur.
Respiratory: Fine crackles bilaterally.
Extremities: Trace lower extremity edema in both legs.

RESULTS
ECG: Stable for the patient. Shows left ventricular hypertrophy, which caused his congestive heart failure.
Echocardiogram: Pumping function of the heart is a little low but stable.
Skin biopsy pathology: Skin cancer was completely removed, and everything is fine.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Shortness of breath, likely exacerbation of congestive heart failure. Probably due to dietary indiscretion with salty food causing fluid retention. Heat exhaustion was also considered initially. Exam shows bilateral fine crackles and trace lower extremity edema, consistent with extra fluid.
- Prescribe an extra dose of Lasix 80 mg once a day.
- Start carvedilol 25 mg twice a day.
- Continue the appropriate medication therapy for heart failure. Echocardiogram and ECG are stable.

2. Elevated blood pressure. Noted in clinic and in the ER report. To be discussed further.

3. Status post cataract removal. Doing well, with no vision problems. No medication adjustment needed.

4. Status post skin cancer removal. Healed well, and pathology shows complete removal. No medication adjustment needed.

The nurse will see the patient shortly.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Low back pain after a lifting injury about four months ago.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Jeremy injured his lower back about four months ago while moving boxes during his son's move out of a college dorm. He thinks it may be a pulled muscle. His appointment was delayed because of scheduling backlogs. He tried physical therapy at his gym without benefit.

At the time of injury, he felt briefly as though he would topple over and could not support his upper body weight. The toes on his right foot tingled for about an hour. The numbness and tingling resolved completely and have not recurred. He reports leg weakness only when carrying something heavy, and he is nervous about lifting heavy objects. He has sharp pain in the lower back with certain movements, such as turning or rolling over in his sleep, which wakes him. The pain resolves when he repositions.

He has tried Tylenol, ibuprofen, heat, and ice without significant relief. Ibuprofen works slightly better than Tylenol but for a shorter duration. He has had no stomach upset from ibuprofen and tries not to take too much.

He was seen at urgent care, where an MRI was recommended. He did not get it because of insurance concerns and because he was starting to feel better. Because symptoms have persisted, he now wants to proceed with the MRI.

He denies bladder or bowel problems, incontinence, and difficulty urinating or defecating. He denies fever and chills.

Past medical history: right total knee replacement in spring 2020. He rehabbed it with PT, and it feels about 95 percent normal.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: No fever or chills.
Genitourinary: No incontinence or difficulty urinating.
Gastrointestinal: No bowel incontinence or difficulty with bowel movements. No stomach upset with ibuprofen.
Musculoskeletal: Low back pain with certain movements. Leg weakness with heavy carrying.
Neurological: Past right toe tingling, resolved. No current numbness or tingling.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Afebrile. BP 117/56. HR 68. SpO2 95% on room air.
Neck: Bony protuberance of C5-C6. No pain to palpation.
Lumbar spine: No pain to palpation. Decreased flexion and extension. Positive straight leg raise. Spasm of the lumbar paraspinal muscles.
Musculoskeletal: Lower extremity strength equal bilaterally.

RESULTS
Lumbar spine X-ray: No acute bony abnormality and no fracture.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Suspected acute lumbar disk herniation. Symptoms have persisted for several months after the injury. The bony prominence at C5-C6 may reflect some arthritis in the neck, and the back findings may reflect residual injury. X-ray shows no fracture but does not evaluate soft tissue.
- Order lumbar spine MRI for better evaluation.
- Refer to physical therapy through the health system.
- Prescribe meloxicam 15 mg once daily.
- If a herniated disk is confirmed, discuss other options such as an epidural steroid injection to reduce inflammation.
- The patient had no questions.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Right foot pain and swelling after dropping a landscape brick on the foot yesterday.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Elijah is a patient referred by his primary care provider after dropping a landscape brick on his right foot yesterday while doing yard work. He initially had some soreness but continued working and moving around. The foot has since become swollen. He wonders whether he has a broken toe. He has not taken any medications such as Tylenol or ibuprofen, saying he does not like taking medicine, and has just been "toughing it out." He rates his pain currently as 11/10. He reports the whole foot is numb, though he says this has been present "for a long time."

Past history: He broke his right ankle about 20 years ago and was treated in a cast. It occasionally gets sore and swells. His other ankle is also sometimes sore, he has had surgery on it, and it may give out occasionally. He is unsure whether this is related to the current injury.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Musculoskeletal: Right foot pain and swelling. Occasional soreness and swelling of the right ankle, and soreness and occasional giving out of the other ankle.
Neurological: Numbness of the whole right foot.
Other systems not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Look good per the doctor (no values given).
Right foot: Bruising on the plantar and dorsal aspects of the foot. Associated swelling. Tenderness to palpation of the midfoot.
Neurovascular: Capillary refill brisk, less than 3 seconds. Strong, bounding dorsalis pedis pulse, symmetric bilaterally. Motor and sensation intact.

RESULTS

Elevated and fluctuating blood pressure readings.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Mr. Thompson is a 67-year-old male with a history of essential hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and osteoarthritis. He reports that his blood pressure has normally been well controlled. He has checked his blood pressure both when feeling fine and during lightheaded episodes, and readings have been on the high side. He describes the lightheadedness as feeling "fuzzy," not spinning. He feels a little unsteady during the dizziness and has a slight headache when readings are higher. He has had occasional heaviness in the chest that is not sustained. He has not had syncope recently.

He is taking lisinopril 20 mg twice daily (increased from once daily at the last visit) and reports very rarely missing doses. He uses a pillbox and has also tried a medication reminder app, which was confusing to set up, but he feels he is staying on schedule accurately. He continues to take atorvastatin for hyperlipidemia. His osteoarthritis is mostly controlled; he is able to golf most of the time but occasionally plays less or skips a day when the weather changes. He takes Tylenol for mild pain and modifies activity as needed.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: No fever.
Cardiovascular: Occasional non-sustained chest heaviness. No palpitations or racing heart. No recent syncope.
Respiratory: No shortness of breath or breathing difficulty.
Gastrointestinal: No nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea.
Neurologic: Lightheadedness ("fuzzy"), mild unsteadiness with dizziness, and slight headache with higher blood pressure readings. Numbness and weakness were asked about; only the unsteadiness and headache were reported.
Musculoskeletal: Mild osteoarthritis pain, controlled with Tylenol.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Cardiovascular: Grade 3/6 systolic ejection murmur, unchanged from prior.
Lungs: Mild bibasilar rales. No wheezes or rhonchi. Good air movement.
Extremities: Trace bilateral lower extremity edema.
Other: Remainder of exam normal and unremarkable.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Essential hypertension, not adequately controlled.
- Increase lisinopril to 60 mg twice daily.
- Start hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily.
- Check blood pressure twice daily for the next 2 weeks.
- Follow up in 2 weeks.
- Stay well hydrated with 6 to 8 glasses of water per day, more if particularly dehydrated or with increased activity in warm weather.
- Limit alcohol; no more than a couple of drinks per week given fluctuating blood pressure.

2. Hyperlipidemia.
- Continue atorvastatin.
- Order cholesterol panel, CBC with differential, comprehensive metabolic panel, and urinalysis (including assessment of kidney function).

3. Osteoarthritis.
- Continue to stay active, such as walking and golfing, without overdoing it.
- Tylenol as needed for mild pain.

Musculoskeletal: Right-sided back pain.

Abdomen: Mild tenderness to palpation. No rebound or guarding.
Back/Flank: Right costovertebral angle (flank) tenderness.

CT of the side/flank: 0.5 cm stone in the proximal right ureter. No evidence of hydronephrosis.

1. Right proximal ureteral kidney stone, 0.5 cm, without hydronephrosis. This is her first stone, with a family history in her father.

- Follow up in 1 to 2 weeks. If symptoms persist, discuss further treatment such as lithotripsy, a minimally invasive procedure using shock waves to break up the stone.
- The patient had no further questions. The nurse will bring in the prescription.

Chronic low back pain for about two years, radiating down the left leg.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Steven reports back pain for about two years. He believes it began after a fall onto his back while playing basketball, and it has hurt ever since. He thinks it may be arthritis. He rates the pain 7/10, sharp, and throbbing at times. Severity varies and he does not know why. The pain radiates down his left leg, and his toes sometimes get numb. He reports intermittent weakness when trying to stand up or after standing for too long. Lying on his side improves the pain, and prolonged standing worsens it. He reports one episode of bowel incontinence over the past two years, which he attributes to standing too long and possibly drinking. It is not a consistent problem. When asked about loss of sensation in the genital or rectal area, he answered "I hope not."

Prior treatments: He received injections from a prior physician (unknown type) and said he had to be held down because he dislikes needles. Physical therapy was not very effective; he felt he could do the same exercises at home, though he said they helped a little. He took a white pill for pain (name unknown) and said it worked. The chart reportedly lists strong pain medication.

Current activity: He is sedentary, sitting at home and watching TV all day. He reports a gain of about 80 pounds over the past year.

Family history: A fourth cousin has scoliosis. He does not think any direct family members have spine conditions.

Social history: He reports having smoked previously but declined to give details. He is not currently smoking.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Musculoskeletal: Positive for chronic low back pain and intermittent weakness.
Neurological: Positive for left leg radiation and intermittent toe numbness.
GI: One episode of bowel incontinence over two years.
Constitutional: Weight gain of about 80 pounds over the past year.
Genitourinary/neurological: Unclear response to questions about genital or rectal sensory loss ("I hope not"). No bladder incontinence was described.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: The doctor reviewed vitals and noted a value in about the 95th percentile range. The specific measure was not stated, and weight/BMI was implied.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm. No murmur appreciated.
Back: No overlying erythema or ecchymosis. Midline tenderness at the L4-L5 disc space with right-sided lumbar paravertebral tenderness. Pain with lumbar flexion and extension.
Supine straight leg raise test positive.
Neurological: Decreased sensation to light touch at the right lateral thigh (L4 dermatome). Patellar and Achilles reflexes symmetric.

RESULTS
MRI: Disc desiccation, disc bulge with paracentral disc herniation resulting in moderate right neural foraminal stenosis.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Chronic lumbar back pain, consistent with L4-L5 herniated disc with radiculopathy, based on symptoms, exam, and MRI. The bulging disc is pinching nerves, which explains the leg symptoms and tenderness.
- Recommend a corticosteroid spinal injection under fluoroscopy. The procedure takes about an hour. If successful, it would be repeated up to about four times a year.
- Because of needle anxiety, an anxiolytic will be prescribed to take about 3 hours before the procedure.
- The patient asked for pain pills. Reassess about a day after the injection, and if pain persists, consider pain medication. The doctor does not want him on long-term pain medication.
- If pain persists after monitoring, surgery may be recommended. The patient does not want surgery, and the plan is to try all other options first.
- The patient will schedule the injection at the front desk.
- The doctor planned to look up the previous pain medication in the chart.
- The patient had no further questions.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Left arm pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Donald Clark is a man born 03/04/1937 who presents with left arm and hand pain. Symptoms began about two weeks ago. He woke at about 2 AM with severe pain. Ice eased it. Sitting on the side of the bed with the arm hanging down did not help. The pain eased by about 4 to 5 AM, and he went back to sleep. This recurred over several nights. After the third episode he saw his primary doctor, who thought it was most likely from a pinched nerve and referred him here.

The pain starts in the hand and travels down the whole arm. On days after a night episode, it usually bothers him some during the day. Moving his neck or shoulder does not bring on the pain. He reports weakness in the hand, including grip. He also reports an old finger injury, and that finger works poorly or only rarely.

His primary doctor gave him numbing medicine, which helped a little. He also received a "neck pill" and gabapentin. Since then, the pain has not bothered him at night. For the last couple of nights his neck has not bothered him, but the hand is still bothering him. He is not sure whether his gabapentin dose is 100 mg or 300 mg, as his lady friend helps manage his medications. He is a veteran with lower extremity neuropathy from the knees to the feet. He initially denied taking blood thinners but later stated he takes Eliquis.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Musculoskeletal: Left arm and hand pain. Mild neck strain with head rotation. No pain with neck or shoulder movement. Mild lateral neck pain on exam.
Neurological: Left hand weakness with decreased grip. Neuropathy of the lower extremities.
Other systems: Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
General: Elderly white man in a wheelchair, no apparent distress.
Neurologic: Reflexes 1+ bilaterally at the biceps, triceps, and brachioradialis. Gait not assessed. Strength and sensation per template for the upper and lower extremities. Sensation to touch felt the same in both hands.
Musculoskeletal: Non-tender over the cervical spine. Mildly restricted cervical extension and right and left lateral rotation, symmetric, causing mild lateral neck pain but no radicular pain. Spurling's maneuver is benign.

RESULTS
Cervical x-ray: Significant disc degeneration at C5-6, and to a lesser extent C4-5 and C3-4. Significant lower lumbar facet arthropathy was dictated as such. C6-7 and C7-T1 are difficult to visualize on the current x-rays. An MRI of the neck is not available. He has had a prior MRI of the lower back.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Left upper extremity neuropathy, suspicious for cervical radiculopathy, with possible contribution from peripheral neuropathy. The doctor suspects a flare of cervical radiculopathy.
2. Neck pain in the setting of arthritis and disc degeneration.

Plan:
- Order a cervical MRI to identify where the nerve roots are compressed. It cannot be done today, and staff will schedule it as soon as possible.
- Tentatively plan a left C7-T1 epidural steroid injection after the MRI, with the exact location pending the MRI results. The patient agreed to the plan.
- Continue gabapentin twice a day and the home exercise program.
- Follow up after the injection to assess relief.
- Blood thinner status: the dictation states he denies blood thinners, but the patient stated during the visit that he takes Eliquis. This discrepancy needs to be clarified before the epidural.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Right flank pain radiating to the groin for two weeks; suspected kidney stone.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient presents with two weeks of pain that starts in the right flank and radiates down to the groin. The pain is intermittent and varies with fluid intake and activity. It is usually 1-2 out of 10 and rises to about 4 out of 10 during exacerbations. He describes it as persistent and never fully going away. He had one episode in which the pain radiated to a testicle, which has since calmed down. He denies dysuria and hematuria. He denies nausea, vomiting, and fever, but reports possible chills. Ibuprofen takes the edge off but the pain persists. He is requesting something stronger for the weekend.

He has a history of kidney stones. He has passed some on his own, usually within a week, and has had surgery a couple of times. All of his family members have had kidney stones. His PCP gave him a strainer, which he has been using without catching a stone so far.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Possible chills. No fever.
Gastrointestinal: No nausea or vomiting.
Genitourinary: Right flank pain radiating to the groin, one episode of pain radiating to a testicle. No dysuria. No hematuria.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Blood pressure mildly elevated, likely related to pain.
Abdomen: No tenderness to palpation.
Back: Right CVA tenderness.
Other: Remainder of the exam described as fine.

RESULTS
CT scan: 0.5 cm stone in the proximal right ureter. No evidence of hydronephrosis.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Right proximal ureteral kidney stone (0.5 cm) without hydronephrosis, in a patient with recurrent nephrolithithiasis and a family history of stones. UTI is possible but felt unlikely.
- Continue pushing fluids to help pass the stone.
- Continue ibuprofen.
- Prescribe tramadol 50 mg for pain. Ibuprofen can be used for breakthrough pain.
- Continue straining urine to catch the stone.
- Order BMP, urinalysis, and urine culture. Antibiotics will be considered based on results.
- Follow up in 1-2 weeks if symptoms persist or the stone has not passed. Further treatment, including possible lithotripsy, will be discussed then. The patient has had lithotripsy before and indicated he would want it.
- The nurse will bring the tramadol prescription. The patient had no further questions.

He is not ready to try medications and is open to suggestions. He denies any thoughts of harming himself or others.

Reflux: He is on omeprazole and has been making lifestyle modifications, cutting back on Red Bull and caffeine. Alcohol intake was tough during the holiday season, but he reports he is better.

Constitutional: Positive for lethargy. Denies fever or chills.
Cardiovascular: Positive for leg swelling. Denies chest pain.
Respiratory: Positive for shortness of breath on exertion. Denies cough.
Gastrointestinal: Denies abdominal pain.
Musculoskeletal: Positive for morning stiffness.
Psychiatric: Positive for depression. Denies suicidal or homicidal ideation.

Vitals: Vital signs look good in the office. Pulse oximetry is good while sitting.

Respiratory: Bilateral crackles at the bases.

Labs: No elevated white blood cell count.

3. Depression.
- Refer to psychiatry for talk therapy.
- No medications at this time.

4. Reflux.
- Continue omeprazole 20 mg daily.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Chest pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Elizabeth is a 53-year-old female with a past medical history of diabetes and high blood pressure (not previously diagnosed in this clinic's system) who presents with chest pain. She reports about 3 months of pressure-like chest pain that occurs when she walks. She describes it as dull, like pressure. It does not radiate. She has been unable to keep up with her walking because of the pain. She wonders whether it might be acid reflux. She has no pain now, and no shortness of breath, sweats, or clamminess now. Per the doctor, there is a family history of heart disease.

Diabetes: She is on metformin. She reports her blood sugars have been a little higher because she has not been able to be active. She is trying to improve her diet but loves sodas. Last hemoglobin A1c was 7. She has an ophthalmology appointment in two weeks for an eye exam. She denies nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or medication side effects from metformin.

Hypertension: Other clinicians have documented elevated blood pressure readings, with a trend running on the high side over the past few years. She has not been told she has high blood pressure, although she mentions someone may have told her before. She is not on any blood pressure medications.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: No sweats or clamminess currently.
Cardiovascular: Positive for exertional chest pressure. No chest pain currently.
Respiratory: No shortness of breath currently.
Gastrointestinal: No nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Neck: No JVD, no swelling, no carotid bruits.
Lungs: Clear, no crackles or rhonchi.
Cardiovascular: 2/6 systolic ejection murmur, noted previously. Otherwise regular rate and rhythm. Pulses equal.
Abdomen: Soft, no tenderness, guarding, or masses.
Back: Normal.
Extremities: 1+ nonpitting edema in the ankle area/lower legs. No calf tenderness.

RESULTS
EKG done in office today: normal, no signs of heart attack.
Prior hemoglobin A1c: 7.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Chest pain, suspected unstable angina. Risk factors include diabetes, suspected hypertension, and family history of heart disease. EKG is normal with no signs of heart attack, but concern remains for a possible blockage.
- Refer to cardiology, with the goal of being seen next week and set up for a stress test.
- Start aspirin 81 mg once daily.
- Prescribe sublingual nitroglycerin. If chest pain occurs with walking, stop; if it resolves with rest, no pill is needed. If pain persists, take a nitroglycerin tablet, wait about 5 minutes, and repeat every 5 minutes up to 3 pills. If the pain is not relieved, call 911 and go to the hospital.
- Return to exercise once cardiac evaluation is complete.

2. Diabetes.
- Continue metformin 500 mg twice daily.
- Order repeat hemoglobin A1c today.
- Keep the ophthalmology appointment for diabetic eye exam.
- Continue to avoid soda and sweets.
- Return in about 2 weeks to consider adjustments.

3. Hypertension, newly added to the problem list, with lower extremity edema.
- Start hydrochlorothiazide (low dose), which may also help with the leg swelling.
- Use a home blood pressure cuff, check daily in the morning on waking, and enter readings in Epic MyChart.
- Diet control measures.
- Counseled on side effects, including increased urination in the evening and possible cross-reaction with sulfa medications. Handout to be provided.
- Follow up in 2 weeks with blood pressure log to adjust medications as needed.

The patient reports staying active during the week, riding a bicycle on trails, including a bike ride over the past weekend. The patient tries to cook fresh food and eat a clean diet most days, but likes chocolate chip cookies. The patient was surprised the cholesterol was high.

Family history: The patient does not talk much with their parents. The grandparents reported no cholesterol problems when they were young. A cousin died at age 44 or 45, thought to be from a heart attack.

Social history: The patient lives alone in an apartment. Parents smoked when the patient lived with them, but no one smokes in the patient's home now, and no one the patient spends time with smokes. The patient has identified as non-gender or non-binary for about two years. The patient thought they were healthy.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Growth: The patient feels they are growing okay.

Vitals: Blood pressure looks good.
Cardiac: No murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Lungs: Clear.
Eyes: No xanthomas appreciated.
Neck: No thyromegaly.
Abdomen: No hepatomegaly or splenomegaly.

RESULTS
Cholesterol level was elevated at 210.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
17-year-old with newly diagnosed hypercholesterolemia. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends screening between ages 9 and 11 and again between ages 17 and 20, which is why the patient was screened; studies show a link between high cholesterol and premature heart attacks. - Perform genetic testing to determine whether this is familial or due to a secondary cause.

- Refer to a nutritionist for dietary guidance.
- Continue regular exercise, including bike riding.
- Discuss tips for achieving the patient's health goals.
- Repeat cholesterol level in 3 to 6 months, after the nutritionist visit and dietary changes.

He was able to get out of the water on his own, but climbing was very sore, and squatting and bending remain painful. This is his first injury to this knee. He denies numbness or tingling in the foot. He has been taking over-the-counter Aleve twice a day and applying a cold pack, which have helped a fair amount, but the knee is still quite sore. He skis frequently, trying to go every weekend, and has plans for a big weekend.

He also has hypertension. He takes lisinopril 20 mg daily and reports no side effects. Home blood pressures have been about 125/80 most days.

Past surgical history: tonsillectomy. No other surgeries noted in the record.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Musculoskeletal: Right knee pain and swelling; pain with squatting and bending.
Neurological: No numbness or tingling in the foot.
Other: No medication side effects from lisinopril.

Vitals: Blood pressure 120/77.
Neck: No lymphadenopathy.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm. No murmur. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses palpable.
Respiratory: Lungs clear to auscultation bilaterally.
Musculoskeletal (right knee): Ecchymosis, edema, and effusion present. Pain to palpation of the medial knee. Decreased range of motion with pain on movement. Negative varus and valgus stress tests. Negative Lachman sign. No other lower extremity edema.

RESULTS
No results available. X-ray and lipid panel ordered (see plan).

1. Right knee pain, likely medial collateral ligament strain.

- Well controlled in office and at home.
- Continue lisinopril 20 mg daily.
- Order lipid panel.

3. Health maintenance.
- Due for tetanus vaccine; administer tetanus shot.

Hypertension: He takes lisinopril 20 mg daily (he believes this is what he takes; "white pill"). He did not buy a blood pressure cuff and does not check his blood pressure. He does not watch his salt intake.

Diabetes: He does not watch his sugar intake and does not check his blood sugars. He takes metformin 1000 mg twice daily as prescribed; his wife fills his pill box and he takes medication twice daily. The physician counseled on the risk of complications such as kidney dysfunction and eye problems.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Right-sided abdominal pain for several weeks; gallstones found on ultrasound. Referred by Dr. Miller.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Bobby is a patient with type 2 diabetes who presents for surgical evaluation of several weeks of abdominal pain. An ultrasound ordered by Dr. Miller showed gallstones. He was advised to avoid high-fat foods but continues to have pain.

The pain is in the right upper abdomen just beneath the ribs. He describes it as squeezing, intermittent, and severe when present, rated 8/10 at its worst. It is associated with nausea but no vomiting. It usually begins immediately after eating, but it can also start a couple of hours after a meal. During episodes of severe pain lasting a couple of days, he has had low-grade fevers. The patient wondered whether it could be a stomach ulcer.

Diet: He is managing type 2 diabetes with diet and exercise. He has cut back on sugar and started a modified keto diet, and he has lost about 25 pounds over 3 months. His blood sugars are improving. He has cut out pork rinds, which were a staple, and says the pain is slightly better but persists.

Family history: Both parents had gallbladder disease and underwent cholecystectomy.

Activity: Exercise is not significantly limited, though he is careful around meals. He enjoys nature photography and is looking forward to getting outdoors in the spring.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Low-grade fevers during severe pain episodes. Weight loss of 25 pounds over 3 months with diet change.
GI: Right upper quadrant abdominal pain related to meals. Nausea. No vomiting.
Other systems: Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: BP 128/88. RR 16. Pulse 68. Afebrile. SpO2 99% on room air.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm. No ectopic beats, clicks, rubs, or murmurs.
Respiratory: Lungs clear and equal bilaterally to auscultation.
Abdomen: Positive bowel sounds. Soft and nondistended. Slight guarding in the right upper quadrant. No rebound tenderness. Positive Murphy's sign with pain on palpation beneath the right ribs on inspiration. No peritoneal signs.

RESULTS
Abdominal ultrasound: Multiple gallstones in the gallbladder with mild gallbladder wall thickening. Common bile duct is normal in size at 4.1 mm.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Mild cholecystitis with cholelithiasis. Symptoms have persisted for several weeks without improvement from dietary modification. There is no frank obstruction. The gallbladder appears inflamed.
- Recommend laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Procedure explained: a few small incisions, with the gallbladder removed through one of them. Expected duration is 1 to 1.5 hours, with an overnight hospital stay for monitoring.
- After surgery, continue to avoid high-fat foods and eat a high-fiber diet.
- Recovery: Take it easy for the first 24 hours. He may walk around on solid ground within a day or two. No hiking initially. Follow-up in about 1 week, with release to resume outdoor activity at that visit.
- The nurse will obtain consent paperwork. Surgery is planned for next week. The patient had no questions.

2. Type 2 diabetes. Follow up with his primary care provider or endocrinologist to ensure diabetes is well managed, particularly given the upcoming surgery. Continue diet and exercise management as outlined by his other providers.

Right knee pain after a skiing injury two weeks ago.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Elizabeth is a patient who injured her knee while downhill skiing two weeks ago. She was skiing a black diamond run and tried to speed past another skier, ran into a tree, and twisted her knee. She heard a pop, which she later clarified was in her left knee. The patient suspects a torn meniscus.

The right knee is the primary source of pain, located on the medial aspect. Her left knee does not really hurt but feels unstable. She rates the right knee pain as 7/10, increasing slowly over the last few days, with episodes reaching 11/10. The worst pain occurs when walking her dog, and it lasts as long as the walk (5 minutes to longer, depending on conditions). Pain is worse with longer walks. She reports a lot of swelling and significant morning stiffness that improves once she starts walking. She cannot ski currently. Moving the kneecap causes a shooting pain down to the ankle but does not hurt the knee itself. She denies frequent radiation of pain otherwise. She reports pain is worse in windy weather.

Treatments tried: a knee brace and THC cream, which she finds helpful. She also takes THC gummies. She has taken no other medications.

Past surgical history: right knee reconstruction at age 14 after feeling a pop doing a back handspring in gymnastics. She has had problems with the knee since then.

Social/activity: formerly a gymnast; skis about three times a week. No other regular exercise.

Medications: none other than THC products.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Musculoskeletal: Right medial knee pain, swelling, and morning stiffness. Left knee instability. Limping.
Neurological: Intermittent shooting pain down to the ankle with kneecap manipulation.
Other systems: Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Right knee: Tenderness to palpation over the medial aspect; no tenderness over the lateral aspect. Mild swelling and bruising of the skin. Able to flex the knee. Patellar movement does not cause knee pain but produces a shooting pain to the ankle. Pain with the movement of the knee away from the body (as described by the doctor); no pain pulling it back toward the body. The doctor described this as pain on dorsiflexion but not plantar flexion.
Gait: Slight limp, with the patient protecting the knee.

RESULTS
X-ray: No fracture. Early development of arthritis.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Posterior cruciate ligament strain, right knee.
- Continue bracing the right knee.
- Physical therapy referral, starting at three times a week to restore strength.
- Avoid skiing and gymnastics for now.
- Meloxicam 15 mg once daily for swelling and bruising.
- Ibuprofen 800 mg twice daily as needed.
- Advised against taking THC gummies at the same time as the medications.

2. Left knee strain, mild.
- No medication or bracing needed.
- Rest and take it easy; listen to her body and let the physical therapist guide activity.

3. Early arthritis on x-ray, which may explain increased joint pain in windy weather.

The patient verbalized understanding and had no questions.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Asthma with frequent cough and wheezing.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Betty is a patient with asthma who reports ongoing frustration with persistent cough and wheezing. Symptoms flare mainly when she gets a cold. She also had one flare after visiting her aunt's house, which she attributes to the aunt's cat, and she has avoided the house since without further problems. She has no history of seasonal allergies. Smoke in bars irritates her, so she tries not to go often.

Over the past six months she has had flares every month or every other month. She has gone to urgent care or her primary care doctor several times this past year and was once seen in the emergency department. She was given antibiotics at times and steroids at times. She almost always needs prednisone, sometimes a high dose over 5 days and sometimes a taper over 9 to 10 days. Her last exacerbation was about a month ago. She was hospitalized once for asthma at about age 8, with no hospitalizations since.

She has two inhalers but uses only the blue albuterol (Ventolin) inhaler, which is the only one that helps. She says the other inhaler does not work when she tries to use it. She uses albuterol almost every day for cough and wheeze, taking two puffs. She wakes a couple of times a week needing it at night, and it usually relieves symptoms enough to let her go back to sleep. She enjoys hiking and wants to get better so she can hike again, but she has to be careful because of her symptoms.

Social history: She has never smoked, and she does not smoke marijuana or vape.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Respiratory: Positive for cough, wheezing, and nighttime awakenings with symptoms.
Allergic/Immunologic: No seasonal allergies.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: BP 128/82. Respiratory rate 16. Oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm. No ectopic beats, rubs, murmurs, or gallops. Strong bilateral pulses. Brisk capillary refill.
Respiratory: Diminished lung sounds throughout with occasional slight expiratory wheeze bilaterally.
Neck: Supple. Trachea midline. No lymphadenopathy. No carotid bruit.
Extremities: No clubbing of the fingertips.

RESULTS
Pulmonary function test done today is consistent with a diagnosis of asthma.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Moderate intermittent asthma
- Start Flovent 110 mcg, one puff twice daily. Consistent use is important to prevent daily symptoms and reduce the need for albuterol. It is not fast acting like albuterol but helps long term.
- Continue Ventolin (albuterol), two puffs every 4 to 6 hours as needed. During an acute exacerbation, use 1 to 2 puffs, wait and reassess breathing, then take an additional 1 to 2 puffs if needed.
- Prepare an asthma action plan to address symptoms and triggers such as cats and dust.
- Follow up in 1 month, sooner if symptoms worsen.

Foot pain after a soccer injury.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Jean is a patient who injured her foot yesterday during a soccer game. While trying to steal the ball, another player fell directly onto her foot and her body twisted around the player. She felt pain in the foot. She stopped playing right away and was helped off the field. (Note: the transcript is inconsistent about laterality. The patient said the other player fell onto her "right" foot, while the doctor and the exam refer to the left foot. The doctor's assessment also mentions "right foot pain" once.) She has had many soccer injuries but has never injured this foot before. She thought it might be a bone bruise.

Since the injury she has been keeping the foot elevated, icing it, and taking ibuprofen. The trainer wrapped it yesterday. Pain is 3/10 with ibuprofen and 7-8/10 without ibuprofen. She denies numbness, tingling, or any strange sensation in the foot. She has played soccer since age 4-5, starting in a local town league and then playing on high school teams.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Neurological: Denies numbness, tingling, or abnormal sensation in the foot.
Musculoskeletal: Foot pain as per HPI.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: BP 118/72, HR 58, RR 14, afebrile, O2 saturation 99% on room air.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm. No clicks, rubs, or murmurs. No ectopic beats.
Respiratory: Lungs clear and equal bilaterally with good air movement.
Left foot: Bruising on the plantar and dorsal surfaces. Associated swelling. Tenderness to palpation of the midfoot. Positive piano key test.
Neurovascular (left foot): Capillary refill brisk, less than 3 seconds. Dorsalis pedis pulse intact and strong. Motor intact. Sensation intact to light touch.

RESULTS
Diagnostic imaging (X-ray) of the foot, reviewed by the doctor: subtle dorsal displacement of the base of the second metatarsal, 3 mm separation of the first and second metatarsal bases, and a bony fragment in the Lisfranc joint space.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Lisfranc fracture of the foot (left per exam; one reference to "right" in the transcript). The fracture involves the second metatarsal where the metatarsals meet the cuboid region.
- Order MRI to assess for ligamentous injury.
- Based on exam and X-ray, surgery is most likely needed. The procedure would reposition the bones and hold them with plates and screws while they heal. It is a same-day surgery.
- After surgery, she will be in a cast and use crutches with no weight bearing on the left foot for about 6-8 weeks. She will then gradually begin walking as tolerated. Follow-up in clinic.
- Risks of not operating were discussed: poor bone and ligament healing, loss of the arch with flat foot deformity, and a high likelihood of arthritis in the foot.
- She will be out for the rest of the season, with the goal of being ready for next season.
- The nurse will start the paperwork. The doctor will see her Monday morning for the procedure.
- The patient agreed with the plan.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Itchy scalp with dandruff.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Barbara is a patient presenting for ongoing scalp itching that she has had for a long time and that has worsened over the past six months or so. She reports significant dandruff/flaking over her clothes, which she finds embarrassing, and she cannot stop itching. She denies rashes elsewhere on her body. She dyes her hair but has done so for years, with no new hair products, sprays, or gels. She has tried over-the-counter treatments including Head & Shoulders and castor oil without improvement. She denies joint pain, fever, or weight loss. Possible family history: her sister reports a dry scalp, though not as severe as the patient's. She reports no new mental or emotional stressors at work or home; things are basically the same.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Denies fever and weight loss.
Musculoskeletal: Denies joint pain.
Skin: Positive for scalp itching and flaking. Denies rashes elsewhere on the body.
Psychiatric: No new stressors.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Blood pressure 130/68, heart rate 98, respiratory rate 18, temperature 97.7. Doctor noted these as normal.
Scalp: Demarcated scaly erythematous plaques present in a patchy distribution, diffusely across the back of the scalp.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Scalp psoriasis. (Eczema was initially considered by the doctor early in the visit; the final impression was scalp psoriasis.)
- Start clobetasol 0.05% solution, applied to affected areas of the scalp and gently rubbed in. Use twice daily (on waking and before bed) during flares.
- Continue T-Gel shampoo for ongoing control.
- Counseled that there is no cure, flare-ups are unpredictable and their cause is not well understood, and the condition will need ongoing management. Use the steroid solution at flares.
- Follow up in three months, or sooner if symptoms worsen significantly. Patient advised to call and come in sooner if worse.
- Patient verbalized understanding of the plan and had no questions.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Annual exam. Recurrent chest pain over the past month.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Evelyn is a 56-year-old female with a past medical history significant for coronary artery disease (prior stenting), prior carpal tunnel release, and a herniated disc. She presents for her annual exam.

Herniated disc: She reports her back has been doing really well. She has had no back pain or limitation in movement. She had a steroid injection several months ago.

Carpal tunnel: She had a release a couple of years ago. She is back at work and has had no issues. She has full range of motion and no numbness or tingling in her hands.

Coronary artery disease: Over the last month she has had intermittent chest pain, located in the middle of the chest. She describes it as burning. It occurs with walking and resolves with rest. She does not get it at rest. It occurs about three times a week. She says it is not severe enough to send her to the ER, but she notices it. She denies shortness of breath, nausea, and vomiting. The physician raised the possibility that it could be acid reflux.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: No fever or chills.
Cardiovascular: Positive for exertional chest pain/burning. No lower extremity edema.
Respiratory: No shortness of breath.
Gastrointestinal: No nausea or vomiting.
Musculoskeletal: No muscle aches. No back pain or limitation in movement.
Neurological: No numbness or tingling in the hands.
HEENT: Positive for nasal congestion from pollen allergies.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Look good per the physician. Blood pressure is well controlled and oxygenation is fine.
Neck: No carotid bruits.
Cardiovascular: Slight 3/6 systolic ejection murmur, which has been heard before.
Respiratory: Lungs clear.
Extremities: No lower extremity edema.
Skin: Healed surgical scars on the right wrist.

RESULTS
Echocardiogram (last year): Ejection fraction slightly low at 45%, which the physician suspects will improve over time. Slight mitral regurgitation, consistent with the murmur heard on exam.
ECG: Stable, reflecting prior coronary artery disease. No new changes.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Carpal tunnel release: Doing well and back at work. No further intervention needed. She will let the physician know if symptoms recur.
2. Herniated disc: Doing well. No referral for further steroid injection or physical therapy at this time. She will let the physician know if symptoms recur.
3. Coronary artery disease with recurrent exertional chest pain: This is the most concerning problem. Continue aspirin and Toprol. Order a cardiac stress test to evaluate for further blockages. Order a lipid panel. Start Crestor 20 mg once daily. The nurse will help schedule the tests, and the physician will be in touch.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Hospital follow-up after admission for heart failure.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Christina is a patient seen for follow-up after a recent hospitalization for heart failure. Before admission she had ankle swelling that did not resolve, including overnight, and difficulty breathing requiring her to be propped up in bed to sleep. She felt very unwell and had difficulty talking. On the advice of a friend she called 911 and was taken by ambulance to the ER. Her blood pressure at that time was 200/90.

She admits she may occasionally miss doses of her medications. She has dietary indiscretion, eating salt and vinegar potato chips daily as home snacking. She was given a water pill in the hospital, which is making her urinate frequently, with near incontinence. A second blood pressure medication was added. She feels somewhat better on these medications but has difficulty remembering to take her pills. She has a home blood pressure cuff but rarely used it; she plans to use it daily now.

Currently she is improving. Shortness of breath is reduced, and she thinks walking more is helping. She is sleeping well. She denies chest pain.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Felt very unwell before admission; improving now.
Cardiovascular: Previously ankle swelling; no chest pain.
Respiratory: Previous orthopnea and dyspnea, now improved; no current shortness of breath problems.
Genitourinary: Frequent urination with near incontinence on diuretic.
Neurologic/Sleep: Sleeping well, no sleep problems.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: BP 128/72, temperature 98.7, heart rate 72, respirations 18, oxygen saturation 96%.
Neck: No jugular venous distention.
Cardiac: 2/6 systolic ejection murmur, previously heard and stable.
Lungs: Clear bilaterally.
Extremities: Trace lower extremity edema.

RESULTS
Echocardiogram: Preserved EF of 55%, abnormal diastolic filling, mild-to-moderate mitral regurgitation.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Congestive heart failure, likely due to dietary indiscretion and uncontrolled hypertension.
- Continue Bumex 2 mg once daily.
- Avoid salty foods and continue to watch diet.
- Keep a log of blood pressures and food intake.
- Weigh daily and call if weight increases by 3 pounds in 2 days.
- Referral to a nutritionist for diet education.

2. Hypertension.
- Continue Cozaar 100 mg daily.
- Continue Norvasc 5 mg once daily.
- Use a pill box or phone alarm to improve medication adherence; take medications consistently.
- Check blood pressure daily at home.
- Order renal artery ultrasound to rule out conditions such as renal artery stenosis.

3. Kidney disease.
- Obtain additional labs to ensure tolerance of the new medications.

Follow-up in 3 months. The patient had no questions.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Bilateral knee pain for about six months.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Julie is referred by her primary care doctor for bilateral knee pain that has lasted about six months. She thinks it could be tendonitis. She cannot recall any specific injury, fall, or inciting event. She describes a deep, achy pain right behind both kneecaps. The pain is worse when standing up after sitting for a while (she works from home at a desk) and with going up and down stairs. She also reports knee pain with squatting. The pain improves after the initial onset of movement. She has taken ibuprofen, Aleve, and occasionally Tylenol, which "take the edge off," but she is never pain free unless she is resting. Any movement, especially rising from sitting, causes pain. She is a avid runner who previously ran five to six miles a day and can now barely run half a mile. She has noticed no redness or swelling of the knees. She has never injured or broken a bone in the knees or elsewhere.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Musculoskeletal: Bilateral knee pain as above. No knee redness or swelling.
No other systems discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: BP 120/70, HR 60, RR 14.
Cardiovascular: Regular rhythm at a slower rate. No murmurs or extra sounds.
Musculoskeletal: Normal gait. Lower extremity strength 5/5 except 3/5 hip abduction bilaterally. Knees: no erythema, ecchymosis, or warmth of the skin. No effusion. Tenderness to palpation. Positive patellar grind test bilaterally. Lachman, anterior drawer, posterior drawer, and McMurray tests negative bilaterally.
Neurological: Patellar and Achilles reflexes symmetric in the lower extremities.

RESULTS
X-rays of both knees: no fractures or osteoarthritis.
MRI done prior to the visit was reviewed by the doctor; no specific findings were stated.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Patellofemoral pain syndrome, bilateral. Symptoms are consistent with this diagnosis, a common cause of knee pain in active people related to how the kneecap tracks along the groove of the femur.
- Continue ibuprofen or other anti-inflammatories (e.g., Aleve) as needed for pain.
- Referral to physical therapy for lower extremity exercises to improve strength and mobility and to correct any faulty running mechanics.
- Take it easy with activity for now. The goal is for the patient to return to running.
- The patient's questions were answered, and she had no further concerns.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Shortness of breath for about one week.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Frank is a patient with a history of coronary artery disease (myocardial infarction in 2018 with stent placed in the right coronary artery), reduced ejection fraction (about 35%), and stage 3 chronic kidney disease. He presents with about one week of shortness of breath. He wonders if it could be pneumonia. He had similar symptoms about six months ago, when his Lasix dose was changed and he improved. He takes Lasix 40 mg once daily and reports taking it every day.

Dyspnea occurs with walking, particularly on stairs and with brisk walking. He has gone from one pillow to two pillows at night. He woke up short of breath six months ago but has not had this episode during the current illness. He reports definite leg swelling. Urination is unchanged, with nocturia once or sometimes twice a night, which he says is a bit more than before and also occurred previously. His diet has not been ideal over the last couple of weeks of holiday family gatherings, with likely excess salt intake.

Kidney: He last saw his nephrologist about a month ago. He has been advised to avoid NSAIDs but took Motrin for a while about a week ago for foot pain and stopped as soon as he could. Tylenol is not very effective for him. No one has previously counseled him about dietary potassium.

Foot pain: About a week ago he had 4-5 days of pain in one foot, just in front of the big toe, which slowly resolved with Motrin. He has no known history of gout.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Respiratory: Positive for exertional shortness of breath. Positive for orthopnea (two pillows). No paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea this episode.
Cardiovascular: Positive for leg swelling.
Genitourinary: No decrease in urination. Nocturia once or twice nightly.
Musculoskeletal: Recent foot pain near the big toe, resolved.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Blood pressure 135/80.
Neck: Jugular venous distention to about 9 cm. No carotid bruits.
Lungs: Bibasilar crackles with occasional rhonchi that clear with cough.
Heart: 3/6 systolic ejection murmur at the left base.
Lower extremities: 1-2+ pitting edema bilaterally.

RESULTS
No results available for review.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Acute heart failure exacerbation, likely related to dietary indiscretion (salt intake).
- Increase Lasix from 40 mg daily to 80 mg daily, taken in the morning. If needed, a second dose can be added in the afternoon around 4 PM, avoiding late-evening dosing.
- Patient to call in two days with weight update.
- Call sooner if shortness of breath worsens; may need admission for IV diuretics.
- Order chest x-ray.
- Strict salt restriction.
- Dietitian referral.

2. Coronary artery disease with history of MI and RCA stent, reduced EF.
- Doing well aside from the heart failure exacerbation.
- Order repeat echocardiogram to evaluate the murmur and reassess ventricular function.
- Doctor to call Dr. White to arrange cardiology follow-up.

3. Stage 3 chronic kidney disease.
- Avoid Motrin and Advil and other NSAIDs. Use Tylenol; call if pain is significant, and alternative medications or therapies will be discussed.
- Order complete metabolic panel to check kidney function.
- Continue follow-up with nephrology.
- Counseled on a low-potassium diet (avoid bananas, oranges, potatoes); dietitian referral placed.

4. Possible gout flare, with a single-foot episode of pain at the base of the big toe.
- Order uric acid level.
- An alternative medication that does not harm kidney function can be discussed.

Patient was reassured that he is expected to improve, and he voiced understanding of the plan.

Not discussed.

Upper respiratory infection symptoms.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Andrew is a 59-year-old male with a past medical history significant for depression, type 2 diabetes, and hypertension who presents with symptoms of an upper respiratory infection. Over the last week or so, while doing yard work and landscaping, he began to feel very tired and short of breath. He reports the shortness of breath occurred with exertion, such as lifting or carrying heavy bags of soil, and he became very winded, which surprised him. He believes he caught a cold that worsened and wonders if it could be the flu. He notes that he has been wearing masks less as the end of summer approached. He has received both COVID vaccines. He has no history of seasonal allergies. He has no cough productive of sputum yet but expects it may be next. He felt a little warm but attributed this to exertion. He reports significant elbow pain and tired knees with some tension around the knees, which he thinks is related to lifting the bags. He denies nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea.

Depression: It has been a "crazy year and a half," and he was somewhat concerned, but overall he has been doing well. His wife got him into barre classes to help him relax, and he feels they are working. Medication was previously deferred because he takes medications for other conditions.

Type 2 diabetes: He monitors his blood sugars on workdays but usually forgets on weekends. His diet has been good for the most part, except for some house parties. His sugars have not been elevated since this episode.

Hypertension: He monitors his blood pressure regularly on workdays but not as much on weekends. He reports it has been under control. He is taking his medication. He needs a refill of lisinopril.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Positive for fatigue. Felt slightly warm, attributed to exertion.
Respiratory: Positive for exertional shortness of breath. No cough productive of sputum yet.
Gastrointestinal: Negative for nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea.
Musculoskeletal: Positive for elbow pain and knee tiredness/tension.
Psychiatric: Depression reportedly well controlled.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Normal per the physician; afebrile.
Cardiovascular: Heart sounds strong.
Respiratory: Scattered rhonchi bilaterally that clear with cough.
Extremities: Mild edema of the lower extremities.
Musculoskeletal: Pain to palpation of both elbows.

RESULTS
Chest x-ray: No airspace disease, no pneumonia.
Diabetic labs: Hemoglobin A1c elevated at 8. Goal is around 6 to 7.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Upper respiratory infection, likely viral syndrome.
- Send COVID test to confirm negative; COVID is not suspected, and there are no known exposures.
- Expected to resolve in a couple of days.
- Robitussin for cough.
- Ibuprofen or Tylenol for fever.
- Patient to report if symptoms worsen.

2. Depression.
- Appears to be doing well with barre classes.
- Offered starting medication or referral to psychotherapy; patient declined for now and will revisit in a few months.

3. Type 2 diabetes, with A1c of 8, above goal.
- Increase metformin to 1000 mg twice daily.
- Repeat hemoglobin A1c in 4 months (ordered).

4. Hypertension, well managed.
- Continue lisinopril 20 mg daily; refill ordered.
- Order lipid panel.

Follow-up: Return in about 4 months; the nurse will assist with scheduling.

Right knee injury after a skiing fall.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Michelle is a patient who injured her right knee last weekend while skiing in Vermont. She caught her ski as she was coming off the lift and fell. She felt her knee pop, and it has hurt ever since. She was unable to bear weight and was taken down the hill by ski patrol, who provided crutches. She reports pain on the outside (lateral) of the knee and a sensation that the knee will not hold her weight and may buckle. She was able to bend the knee immediately after the injury but not really now. She can straighten it somewhat, but straightening all the way is very painful. She denies numbness or tingling in her toes and thinks she can feel her toes normally. She is taking ibuprofen, which helps somewhat. She declined something stronger for pain. She is otherwise generally healthy, with no history of hypertension or diabetes. She is the mother of 2 four-year-old twins and chases them for activity. She would like to return to running but is currently not very active. Her husband is home but works a job that takes him away often, so she is largely alone with the children. An x-ray of the right knee was previously done.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Musculoskeletal: Right knee pain, instability or buckling sensation, decreased range of motion, pain with full extension.
Neurological: No numbness or tingling in the toes.
Other systems: Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm. No murmur.
Respiratory: Lungs clear to auscultation.
Right knee: Edema and effusion present. Pain to palpation of the lateral knee. Decreased flexion and extension. Positive Lachman sign.
Vascular: Palpable dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses. No leg or ankle edema.

RESULTS
X-ray of the right knee: No bony abnormality.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Right knee injury, concerning for anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) rupture, based on mechanism of injury, instability, effusion, and positive Lachman sign. Given the significant lateral knee pain, other structures may also be injured, and the doctor mentioned a possible meniscus tear early in the visit. The doctor noted that the ACL can be torn even when the physical exam is normal.
- Order MRI of the right knee, hoping to complete it within the next couple of days, to confirm the exam findings and evaluate for other structural damage. Discuss further management after the MRI, including graft choice if ACL repair is needed.
- Continue ibuprofen 600 to 800 mg every 8 hours as needed for pain.
- Place the knee in a brace for support.
- Continue using crutches.
- Follow up after the MRI. The patient had no questions.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Non-healing wound on the right foot.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Wayne is a patient with diabetes and neuropathy who presents with a wound on the right foot for the past 2 to 3 weeks that is not improving. He was referred by his PCP. He previously saw a podiatrist but that provider moved away and he was unable to find another. He denies any trauma. He bought a new pair of shoes (Hokas) for travel and, because of neuropathy, did not feel that they were too tight. It started as a blister and now looks much worse. He has been covering it with a Band-Aid. He thinks it could be athlete's foot. He completed a course of antibiotics prescribed by his PCP yesterday, and the wound looked about the same. He denies pain because he cannot feel the wound. He denies fever, chills, or drainage, but reports that his sock sometimes sticks to the wound even with a Band-Aid. He is no longer wearing the shoes that caused the problem. He likes them because they are comfortable, easy to take on and off, and provide good stability; he reports occasional issues with stability. Regarding his diabetes, he does not think it is too bad. His last hemoglobin A1c was a little over 8.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Denies fever and chills.
Musculoskeletal/Skin: Right foot wound as per HPI. Sock sticks to the wound at times.
Neurological: Neuropathy with decreased sensation in the foot. Reports occasional stability issues.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Temperature 98.1, heart rate 72, respirations 16, blood pressure 110/65.
Vascular: Palpable bilateral femoral and popliteal pulses. No palpable DP or PT pulses, but Doppler signals are present.
Foot: 1 x 2 inch circular wound on the dorsal aspect of the lateral right foot, just proximal to the right fifth MTP joint. Yellow slough present with minimal granulation tissue. No surrounding erythema or cellulitis. No fluid collection, necrosis, or odor. No bony exposure appreciated. Non-tender to palpation per patient.

RESULTS
Right foot x-ray: No evidence of osteomyelitis (no evidence of bone infection).
Last hemoglobin A1c (patient reported): a little over 8.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Diabetic foot ulcer, right foot
- Order ankle brachial index (ABI) to assess blood supply and ability to heal the wound.
- Debridement of devitalized tissue performed in the office.
- Prescribe collagenase ointment applied to the wound once daily, covered with a dry sterile dressing. Continue until the wound is shrinking and healthy pink tissue is present.
- Surgical shoe to offload pressure from the area.
- No further antibiotics needed at this time.
- Follow up in 2 weeks. May refer to a vascular specialist if the ABI shows blood supply is not optimal for healing.

2. Diabetes mellitus
- Glycemic control is important for wound healing. Last A1c was a little over 8.
- Consider a diabetic (nutrition) consult for dietary modifications to improve hemoglobin A1c.

The patient had no further questions.

Back pain.

Hematuria. Established patient presenting for renal ultrasound.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Kelly Wood is a woman (DOB 02/15/1979) and an established patient seen for evaluation of hematuria. For the past six weeks she has had a few episodes of bright red urine, described as the color of cherry Kool-Aid. Last week, after scheduling this appointment, she passed what looked like two small stones. Last week she also had urinary frequency with constant urge to void and severe painful urination. She rated the pain at that time as 8/10. Since passing the stones she feels much better and denies current flank pain or low back tenderness. The doctor raised the possibility of a bladder infection. She reports drinking little water and drinks more Mountain Dew than anything else. Current medication: Alavert 10 mg daily. No drug allergies. Kidney stone risk factors and prevention were discussed previously.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Genitourinary: Positive for hematuria, urinary frequency, and dysuria last week (now improved). Positive for passage of stones. Hematuria has nearly subsided.
Musculoskeletal: Denies current flank pain or low back tenderness.
Other systems: Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Abdomen: No flank pain.
Genitourinary: Normal vaginal exam.
(Exam performed using the doctor's default physical exam template, updated for the above.)

RESULTS
Urine dipstick: Negative for leukocytes, nitrates, protein, ketones, bilirubin, and glucose. Color yellow and clear. Urobilinogen 0.2, pH 5.5, specific gravity 1.020. Trace blood, intact.

Renal ultrasound:
- Right kidney: 10 cm long by 5 cm wide. No stones, masses, or hydronephrosis.
- Left kidney: 10.8 cm long by 5 cm wide. 6 mm non-obstructing left renal stone.
- Bladder: pre-void volume 533 mL, post-void volume 0 mL.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Hematuria (primary diagnosis): Attributed to kidney stones. The patient passed two stones last week and the bleeding has nearly subsided.
2. Chronic urolithiasis (secondary diagnosis): One 6 mm non-obstructing stone remains in the left kidney. It is not causing pain, so no surgical intervention is recommended at this time.

Prevention counseling:
- Stone formation has no single cause. Risk factors include dehydration, family history, certain foods, digestive tract disease, and certain medical conditions.
- Drink about half of body weight in ounces of water daily (e.g., 125 oz for 250 lb). Avoid sugary drinks such as Mountain Dew.
- Limit sodium to less than 1,000 mg per day and avoid salty, processed foods. Reduce animal protein (beef, poultry, fish, pork).
- Avoid oxalate-rich foods such as spinach, chocolate, beets, rhubarb, and soy products.
- A handout on dietary recommendations was provided.

Follow-up: Return in one year if no further bleeding or pain. She should call the office sooner for any issues. She should go to the emergency room for severe pain or bright red blood in the urine.

She was trying to volley the ball, got in front of another player, and fell on top of her foot. She twisted around while trying to catch herself and then felt pain in the foot. She thought it might be a bone bruise. She could not continue playing and had to be helped off the field because she could not bear weight on the foot. She previously injured her left foot, not the right.

Since the injury she wrapped the foot with an ace wrap after the game, iced it last night, kept it elevated on a pillow, and took ibuprofen. Ibuprofen helps a little but wears off after a while. She denies numbness, tingling, or loss of sensation and can still feel her foot. She plays tennis recreationally with friends to work out.

Neurological: No numbness, tingling, or loss of sensation.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: BP 125/70, respiratory rate 18, temperature 97.1, SpO2 100%, pulse about 60 bpm.
Cardiovascular: No murmur, rub, or gallop. Regular rate and rhythm.
Lungs: Slight stridor appreciated. No wheezes or rales.
Abdomen: No rebound or guarding.
