Brittany is a patient who presents with right foot pain that began about a couple of days ago while playing doubles tennis. She was trying to volley the ball, got in front of another player, and fell on top of her foot. She twisted around trying to catch herself and then felt pain in the foot. She was unable to continue playing and had to be helped off the field because she could not bear weight on the foot. She previously injured her other (left) foot, but has not injured the right foot before. Since the injury she wrapped the foot with an Ace wrap, iced it last night, kept it elevated on a pillow, and took ibuprofen. Ibuprofen helps a little, but the relief wears off after a while. She denies numbness, tingling, or loss of sensation and can still feel her foot. She plays tennis recreationally with friends to work out and is trying to learn. She is right-handed and wants to return to playing tennis.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Neurological: Denies numbness, tingling, or loss of sensation in the foot.
Musculoskeletal: Right foot pain and inability to bear weight after the injury.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: BP 125/70, respiratory rate 18, temperature 97.1, SpO2 100%, pulse about 60 bpm.
Cardiac: No murmur, rub, or gallop. Regular rate and rhythm.
Lungs: A little stridor appreciated. No wheezes or rales.
Abdomen: No rebound or guarding.
Head/skin: Head symmetrical. Mucous membranes normal. Not hot to touch.
Right foot: Bruising of the plantar and dorsal aspects of the foot with associated swelling. Tenderness to palpation of the midfoot. Positive piano key test of the first and second metatarsals. Warm to touch.
Right foot neurovascular: Capillary refill less than 3 seconds, strong dorsalis pedis pulse, sensation intact to light touch.
Left foot: Normal exam. Capillary refill appropriate, pedal pulses strong, sensation intact.

RESULTS
X-ray of the right foot: Subtle dorsal displacement of the base of the second metatarsal, with a 3 mm separation of the first and second metatarsal bases and a bony fragment in the Lisfranc joint space.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Right foot pain consistent with a Lisfranc fracture (second metatarsal region near the top of the foot), based on exam and x-ray.
- Surgery recommended to reposition the bones using plates and screws and to prevent complications. Without surgery there is a risk of poor bone alignment or poor ligament healing, which can lead to loss of the arch (flat foot) and arthritis in the foot.
- The patient was fearful of surgery and asked questions about it. She was counseled that it is a day surgery, not a long procedure, with same-day discharge.
- MRI ordered to further assess the fracture and any ligament injury.
- After surgery she will be in a cast and on crutches, with no weight bearing on the foot for 6 to 8 weeks, then gradual return to walking based on progress.
- Clinic follow-up in about 1 week after surgery.
- She will not be able to drive because it is her right foot and will need someone to take her home.
- She will be out for the rest of the tennis season. Physical therapy recommended after surgery to strengthen muscles and prepare her for return to play.
- Surgical risks (bleeding, loss of sensation, nerve damage) will be reviewed with paperwork and by staff. She was encouraged to ask questions before and after the procedure.
- The patient verbalized understanding.

Right knee pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Abigail is a runner who jogs, signs up for 5Ks, and sometimes runs marathons. She reports right knee pain that has been going on for a while. The knee aches when she runs, and she has not been doing longer distances because of it. The pain is worse toward the end of the day after being on her feet all day, starting in the afternoon. Ice, rest, and ibuprofen make it feel better. Running and activity make it worse. She has discussed this with her primary care provider, Dr. Wood, over the years, and at her last visit he referred her to this office. She has no family history of arthritis or immune disease that she can think of.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Musculoskeletal: Right knee pain as above. Left knee feels normal.
Neurological: No numbness or tingling in the feet.
Constitutional: No fever noted at presentation.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Blood pressure 120/60. Heart rate 58. Respiratory rate 14. Afebrile.
Cardiovascular: Heart sounds good.
Respiratory: Lungs sound good.
Musculoskeletal: Left knee has normal movement without pain. Right knee has no redness or swelling. A small effusion is present. Tenderness to palpation is on the lateral (outside) aspect of the right knee. Resisted extension and flexion of the right knee are not painful.
Neurovascular: Pedal pulse is good. Sensation in the feet is intact, with no numbness or tingling.

RESULTS
X-rays of the right knee, obtained this morning and reviewed by the doctor: joint spaces are well maintained, no evidence of fracture, and no signs of arthritis. Comparison with the left knee looks good.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

- Weight lifting and squats at the gym are acceptable. She should attend the first physical therapy appointment for guidance on the best exercises.
- Follow up in 2 weeks to reassess. If improving, activity will be added gradually. She will schedule the appointment at the front desk.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Evaluation of abnormal renal ultrasound with an atrophic right kidney.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Ashley James is a 14-year-old female (DOB 12/27/2006), previously healthy, who presents with her parents for evaluation of an atrophic right kidney.

History per mother: Ashley came home one day acutely ill with right-sided abdominal pain severe enough that she was bent over. She was treated for a presumed stomach virus with fluids and sent home, and the next day she was twice as bad. A repeat visit included an ultrasound, which showed one kidney was bigger. A brief primary care follow-up did not change management, and she continued to have vomiting and significant pain. She was seen in Jacksonville, where she was told the right kidney was atrophic, much smaller than the other, and not thought to be working. Cysts were reported on the kidney, ovaries, and possibly other areas. Lymph nodes were swollen and infection was found. Because she did not improve and her primary doctor was out of town, the family came to Atlanta, where she was seen and treated over about 4 days. She improved afterward and has had no further vomiting, but continues to complain of abdominal pain and burning, especially when eating.

Currently, Ashley reports mild abdominal pain with some burning. She sometimes has difficulty starting urination. She has not noticed blood in her urine. Per mother, she has burning with urination after certain drinks such as soda, so she drinks only Gatorade or water.

Past medical history: She was healthy before this illness. It was suggested she may have had a severe infection at some point that affected her kidney. At age 4 she was hospitalized 3-4 times, sometimes for 3 days, with fever and infection symptoms. She was given fluids and antibiotics, and no source was identified. This recurred every week or two for a couple of months and then stopped. She has had no problems since. She has seen GI and genetics, and the genetic panel showed no clinically significant mutations. No pregnancy or delivery complications.

Medications: Pepcid 40 mg daily and Claritin for allergies.

Family history: Renal disease in her father, great aunt, and cousins. Her father had a congenital obstructive condition affecting urination that was not caught in time and led to chronic kidney disease, dialysis, and a failed transplant. His cause of death was discussed and clarified at the end of the visit as dialysis-related in his 40s rather than a heart attack, though the record was not fully reconciled. A paternal great aunt had end-stage renal disease, CKD stage 5, diabetes, and hypertension as an adult. Her maternal side includes breast cancer in her mother.

Social: Active in softball and wants to join the drill team over the summer.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Gastrointestinal: Mild abdominal pain and burning, worse with eating. No further vomiting.
Genitourinary: Occasional hesitancy starting urination. Dysuria with carbonated drinks. No hematuria.
Other systems not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
General: Well-appearing female, alert and oriented, sitting comfortably, in no acute distress.
Cardiovascular: Heart sounds normal.
Respiratory: Lungs sound normal.
Remainder of exam within normal limits.

RESULTS
Outside records and multiple kidney images were reviewed. Per the doctor, kidney function looks good and blood pressure is normal. Right kidney is smaller, with the left appearing larger, possibly from compensatory work. Prior genetic panel showed no clinically significant mutations. No specific values were given.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
14-year-old female with an atrophic right kidney and probable compensatory enlargement of the left kidney. Kidney function and blood pressure are currently normal. She is at higher risk for hypertension and proteinuria. No intervention is needed today.

Plan:
1. Annual monitoring: kidney ultrasound for size and function, urinalysis for protein and blood, and blood pressure check.
2. Avoid NSAIDs such as ibuprofen. Use Tylenol instead.
3. Maintain hydration, at least 2 liters of water per day, especially during sports, to avoid dehydration.
4. Healthy diet and continued active lifestyle.
5. Family renal records provided by mother will be reviewed.
6. Next follow-up may be with her primary care physician or an adult nephrologist closer to home.
7. Family to call the office or primary care with questions or if symptoms worsen.

No results available. Imaging and labs not yet obtained.

- Recheck hemoglobin A1c.
- Refill metformin 500 mg; continue current dose.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Abdominal pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Barbara is a 31-year-old female with a history of type 2 diabetes and asthma who presents with one week of abdominal pain. The pain is gradually increasing in severity. It is located in both sides of the upper abdomen. It worsens with exercise such as jogging or running, so she has been taking it easy. She has had intermittent nausea about three times in the past week and has vomited a couple of times. She denies fever. She reports increased coffee intake starting last week, heaviest toward the end of the week, and has cut back this week to about one cup. She also reports eating a lot of spicy food lately. She wonders whether these have triggered gastritis. The doctor notes a moderately heavy history of alcohol use.

Diabetes: She feels it is under control. She reports a blood sugar value of "eight hundred" (as transcribed; value unclear). She is taking metformin 500 mg twice daily, increased at the last visit, which she feels is helping.

Asthma: She has had no recent asthma attacks. She is prescribed Flovent twice daily and albuterol as needed for wheezing. She sometimes forgets Flovent doses and has considered decreasing it because she has had no attacks.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: No fever.
Gastrointestinal: Positive for abdominal pain, intermittent nausea, and vomiting. Diarrhea was asked about and not clearly answered.
Respiratory: No recent asthma attacks.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Cardiovascular: Grade 3/6 systolic ejection murmur, unchanged from prior exam. Otherwise normal heart exam.
Respiratory: Mild, very faint end-expiratory wheezes. Otherwise normal lung exam with excellent air movement.
Abdomen: Mild epigastric tenderness. Abdomen otherwise soft. No right lower quadrant tenderness. No significant right upper quadrant tenderness.
Other: Remainder of the exam is unremarkable.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Abdominal pain, acute gastritis, likely related to caffeine intake and possibly alcohol and spicy food.
- Cut back on caffeine, alcohol (keep to fewer than 2-3 drinks per week), and spicy food.
- Prescription for Zantac (ranitidine) twice daily for stomach acid and pain.
- Order urinalysis, urine pregnancy test, CBC, and comprehensive metabolic panel to rule out other causes.

2. Type 2 diabetes.
- Continue metformin with a dose adjustment: 1000 mg in the morning and 500 mg in the evening.
- Continue checking blood sugars and bring the readings to the next visit.
- Follow up in four weeks.

3. Asthma.
- Continue Flovent daily, as daily use decreases the frequency of attacks. Use albuterol as needed.
- Advised against decreasing Flovent.

Follow-up in four weeks, sooner if questions or concerns.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Evaluation of newly diagnosed ovarian cancer.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient has a past medical history of type 2 diabetes and presents for evaluation of newly diagnosed ovarian cancer. She reports feeling "pretty good" but depressed. Symptoms that prompted workup were severe pain and bleeding. She also reports constipation and weight loss. She denies vomiting. The doctor also asked about urinary issues, but the patient did not address them.

Gynecologic history: menarche at age 13, menopause at age 28 (as stated by the patient). She has never been pregnant and has no children. She is not taking oral hormone replacement therapy. No history of endometriosis. Family history of gynecologic cancers is unknown because she was adopted.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Positive for weight loss.
Gastrointestinal: Positive for constipation. Negative for vomiting.
Genitourinary: Positive for vaginal bleeding and pain.
Psychiatric: Reports feeling depressed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Abdomen: Slight tenderness to palpation of the left lower quadrant. No rebound or guarding. Mass felt on the left side.
Genitourinary: No external lesions on the labia. Vaginal vault within normal limits. Cervix is pink without lesions. Bimanual exam reveals a left adnexal mass. No masses on the right.

RESULTS
Abdominal CT: 3 cm left ovarian mass with associated localized lymph node involvement. No evidence of gross peritoneal or metastatic disease.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Ovarian cancer, most likely, with CT findings suggestive of stage IIIA disease based on lymph node involvement. History of type 2 diabetes.
- Blood tests: CA-125, hCG, AFP, and LDH to help determine tumor type.
- Genetic counseling and testing for genetic predisposition to ovarian cancer.
- Treatment is surgery followed by adjuvant chemotherapy, starting after recovery from surgery.
- Surgery: hysterectomy, removal of both ovaries, and lymph node dissection of involved nodes and any others seen. Tissue from any suspicious areas will be sent for pathology. Final staging will be based on pathology reports.
- Chemotherapy with cisplatin and Taxol. Depending on surgical findings, intraperitoneal chemotherapy may be recommended, delivered through a small tube placed into the abdomen.
- Patient asked whether she will die. The doctor counseled that the prognosis appears favorable and that she is young and healthy, which improves her prognosis. A definitive answer requires the final pathology report. The patient voiced understanding.

2. Depressed mood in the setting of new diagnosis. Acknowledged and supported during the visit. No specific plan discussed.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Right ankle pain after a fall.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Carolyn is a patient who presents with right ankle pain that began yesterday. She slipped on ice while taking out the trash, fell, and is fairly sure she heard a pop. Initially she could not bear weight and a friend helped her inside. Today she can put a little more weight on the ankle but is still limping. She iced and elevated the ankle last night and took ibuprofen last night and this morning before the visit. Her pain is currently 4/10 with ibuprofen and about 6/10 without it. With ibuprofen it goes down to about 1/10 at best. She has had many prior injuries to her ankles but has never injured this right ankle before. She played soccer in college and plays intramural soccer now, but has not been able to play since the injury. She denies numbness or tingling in the right foot.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Musculoskeletal: Right ankle pain and limping as above.
Neurological: Denies numbness or tingling in the right foot.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Reported as looking good.
Right ankle: Ecchymosis over the lateral malleolus with associated edema. Tenderness to palpation of the anterior lateral soft tissue. No laxity on anterior drawer or inversion stress testing. No bony tenderness on palpation of the foot or ankle.
Neurovascular, right foot: Brisk capillary refill in less than 3 seconds. Strong dorsalis pedis pulse. Sensation intact to light touch. Findings are consistent with the left side.

RESULTS
X-ray of the right ankle: No fracture.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Right ankle pain, consistent with a sprain of the lateral ligament complex, specifically the anterior talofibular ligament, which was stretched in the fall.
- Elevate the leg when seated and continue icing.
- Air cast provided to stabilize the ankle.
- Crutches prescribed. Stay off the leg for now, then begin walking as tolerated in a couple of days.
- Continue ibuprofen or other NSAIDs as needed for pain and to reduce inflammation and swelling.
- Symptoms should improve significantly over a few weeks.
- Follow up in 14 days.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Left ankle pain after a fall. Also follow-up for diabetes and hypertension.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Stephanie Morales is a 36-year-old female with a history of diabetes and hypertension who presents with left ankle pain. Two days ago she slipped on snow and ice while walking to her car, and her left ankle turned underneath her. She clarified that the injury was more on the outside of the ankle. She fell to the ground. She was able to get up, but the ankle was very sore, then became swollen and painful, and it is hard to walk. She has tried ibuprofen, ice, and elevation with a little relief. She denies pain above the ankle in the calf, lower leg, or knee; the pain is mostly over the outside of the ankle. She reports swelling but no bleeding. She wonders whether she may have a torn tendon.

Diabetes: She takes metformin. She reports her blood sugars have been stable with diet, and she checks them regularly. The last hemoglobin A1c on record was about 6.8. She has been working on cutting out sweets and sugars and on exercise. She is due for a diabetic eye exam in the next couple of weeks and already has an appointment.

Hypertension: She takes Norvasc and needs a refill. No issues were reported. The doctor had not seen her in about a year.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Musculoskeletal: Left ankle pain and swelling, difficulty walking. No calf, lower leg, or knee pain.
Skin: No bleeding.
Endocrine: Blood sugars stable.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Blood pressure 120/70.
Neck: Normal, no bruits.
Lungs: Clear.
Cardiac: Normal exam. 2/6 systolic ejection murmur, previously present and unchanged.
Abdomen: Normal.
Left ankle: Tenderness over the lateral malleolus and over the fifth metatarsal. Swelling and redness present. Pain with valgus stress of the ankle. Sensation normal. Pulses normal.

RESULTS
Previous hemoglobin A1c was about 6.8 (per chart review). No new results.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Left ankle injury, likely ankle sprain. Fracture is a concern because of tenderness over the fifth metatarsal.
- Order left ankle x-ray.
- Place in air splint and provide crutches. Avoid weightbearing until the x-ray results are back.
- Start Naprosyn 500 mg twice daily for pain.
- Continue elevation and ice.
- If the x-ray shows a fracture, the patient will be called and referred to orthopedics. If there is no fracture, remove the air splint and begin partial weightbearing as tolerated.

2. Diabetes.
- Continue metformin.
- Order repeat hemoglobin A1c and baseline labs today.
- Keep the scheduled eye exam appointment.
- Call with any issues.

3. Hypertension. Blood pressure is well controlled today.
- Refill Norvasc.
- Continue to monitor and call if anything changes.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Follow-up on anxiety after starting Buspar, and follow-up on breast lumps. Pap smear discussed.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Donna Torres is a 40-year-old female (DOB 08/01/1980) presenting for follow-up.

Anxiety: Dr. Brown recently started Buspar, which is new for her. She reports her anxiety is now going well. It was severe in November and December. Initially it spiked the week before her period, then progressed to random spikes with no apparent reason, usually starting during the day at work. Dr. Ward had started Singulair and cautioned that it can cause anxiety, so she is unsure whether it contributed. She wonders about a thyroid problem. The doctor raised a possible hormonal component, noting irritability before progesterone was started (started for period regulation), though the patient was on progesterone in November and December, so a clear link is uncertain. Other contributors discussed include aging and work stress: the "golive" in November and December, and her role leading delivery of COVID results to patients, with the opening of evaluation centers and a COVID clinic. She felt guilty and selfish for having anxiety because she was not on the front lines.

Weight/appetite: She has not intentionally lost weight but reports losing some weight over the past six months. She stopped Camila birth control because of markedly increased hunger and constant eating, and she now feels better. The doctor noted her face appears thinner.

Breast lumps: She has persistent breast lumps that feel smaller but are still present. She has tenderness in the area where the doctor palpated, which she says was also sore when she was breastfeeding (history of a clog). Family history: mother diagnosed with breast cancer at almost 45. She is worried because she is almost 40.

Vulvar itching/discomfort: She uses a cream once a week, which helps. She needs her first refill.

Preventive care: Last Pap was in 2019, negative/negative. She had an abnormal Pap around 2009 and was followed every six months for a while before a normal Pap. She has had the COVID vaccine, as has her son (first dose). Her husband and daughter are not ready to be vaccinated.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Weight loss over the past six months. Increased hunger, now resolved after stopping Camila.
Breast: Lumps with tenderness.
Genitourinary: Vulvar itching/discomfort, improved with cream.
Psychiatric: Anxiety, improved. Prior irritability.
Other: No other issues reported.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Neck: Small bumps palpable, which the patient says are smaller than before.
Breast: One breast feels a little denser, with tenderness at the palpated area. Lumps persist.
Genitourinary: Exam of the vulvar area looks good.

RESULTS
Not discussed. Prior Pap in 2019 was negative/negative.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Anxiety: Improved on Buspar. Likely multifactorial (possible hormonal contribution, stress, aging). Continue Buspar.
2. Breast lumps, tender, with family history of breast cancer (mother at almost 45): Lumps are stable to smaller, and there has been no change. Findings are likely benign (cysts, fibroadenomas), and the doctor explained that cancer would be expected to show change. Continue monitoring. Given the patient's worry, refer to a breast specialist, who may perform in-office ultrasound and earlier procedures if needed. Referral will be sent, and the office will call to schedule within a couple of business days.
3. Cervical cancer screening: Repeat Pap given history of abnormal Pap in 2009 and the doctor's observed increase in abnormal Paps during the pandemic.
4. Vulvar itching/discomfort: Continue cream once weekly. Refill needed.
5. Weight loss over six months: Noted. Patient stopped Camila because of increased hunger and is feeling better.

The patient has no further questions. She will call if anything else is needed.

Nonhealing right foot ulcer.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Christina is a patient with type 2 diabetes who presents with a nonhealing foot ulcer present for about one year. There was no trauma. It started as a small blister that she picked at, and it became red and infected. She saw her primary care provider and was treated with antibiotics (Keflex), and it seemed to improve, but nothing has made it resolve. Her last antibiotic course was about five months ago. She reports no pain but has decreased sensation in the foot. Lately there has been significantly more drainage from the wound, and she feels a little more tired. Blood sugars are running better than before but are still in the 200s. Her last A1c was about 10. She is reportedly on metformin and insulin per the doctor's statement. She has been wearing regular shoes. She plans to walk around the zoo this weekend and eat out, contrary to her PCP's recommendations.

Constitutional: Positive for fatigue. No fever or chills reported.
Skin: Positive for increased wound drainage.
Neurological: Decreased sensation in the foot. No pain in the foot.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Look good; afebrile.
Right foot: 1 x 2 cm circular wound on the dorsal aspect of the lateral right foot, just proximal to the fifth MTP joint. Yellow slough present with minimal granulation tissue. No surrounding erythema or cellulitis. No fluid collection. No necrosis. No odor. No bony exposure. Non-tender to palpation.

RESULTS
X-ray of right foot: No evidence of osteomyelitis.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Diabetic foot ulcer, right lateral foot, present about one year. Possible peripheral artery disease is considered given the chronicity. Neuropathy is consistent with diabetes.
- Order ankle brachial index (ABI) to assess blood supply and healing potential.
- Debridement of the ulcer in the office today.
- Prescribe collagenase ointment applied to the wound once daily and covered with a sterile dressing, continued until the wound begins to shrink.
- Provide a surgical shoe to offload pressure; advised to limit pressure on the foot, including during the weekend zoo trip.
- Follow up in two weeks for reassessment and possible repeat debridement.

2. Type 2 diabetes, uncontrolled, with A1c about 10 and glucose in the 200s.
- Advised to follow up with PCP regarding glycemic control and medication management.

He denies genital or rectal sensory loss, weakness, and loss of bladder or bowel control.

He tries to stay active but this has been difficult due to pain, and he has gained weight over the past years. He had recently started playing golf and the pain has set him back.

Family history: no known family members with spine conditions.
Social history: former smoker, quit about 20 years ago.

Musculoskeletal: Positive for chronic back pain. Negative for weakness.
Neurological: Positive for numbness and tingling in the right leg and foot. Negative for genital or rectal sensory loss.
GU/GI: Negative for loss of bladder or bowel control.

Vitals: Reviewed, overall look good.
Musculoskeletal (back): No overlying erythema or ecchymosis. Midline tenderness at the L4-L5 disk space with right-sided lumbar paravertebral tenderness. Pain with lumbar flexion. Supine straight leg raise test positive.

Follow-up after hospitalization at District Regional Hospital (06/29/2021 to 07/02/2021) for suspected urinary tract infection, constipation, and autonomic dysreflexia symptoms. The patient also wants to discuss COVID-19 vaccination.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Michelle King is a 39-year-old female (DOB 05/07/1982) with a history of quadriplegia from a prior spinal cord injury and a suprapubic catheter. She was admitted on 06/29/2021 and discharged on 07/02/2021. She presented to the emergency department with increasing spasms, lightheadedness, significant constipation, and diaphoresis. In the ED she was febrile with a white blood cell count of 23,000. There was concern for ongoing urinary tract infection, and she was treated with IV antibiotics. She also had labile blood pressure, headache, and vomiting. She improved slowly and was discharged after clinical improvement. Cultures were obtained and reviewed.

At today's visit, the patient states she does not think this was a UTI. She believes she was constipated and that the constipation caused her high blood pressure. She had hardly any bowel movements in the hospital. After going home she had a very large bowel movement and felt much better. She told the hospital team this, and they obtained x-rays but did not think constipation was the cause. She went to the ER because her blood pressure was out of control, causing headache and vomiting, and she had exhausted what she could do at home. She feels she is back to her normal self and is otherwise doing well. She denies pain or discomfort.

She had not had a regular bowel movement in a while before admission, despite taking Miralax daily. When she does not go, she doubles the Miralax. She has lactulose, which takes about two days to work and is very unpleasant. It was extremely hot and humid in the last two weeks of June. She tends to stay indoors more in the heat.

COVID-19 vaccine: she is unvaccinated. She is concerned about unknown side effects and "vaccine injury." She feels she is young and healthy enough to fight the infection, even with limited respiratory function. She takes vitamin C and multivitamins and is closely monitored. She does not receive an annual flu shot. She says she is open-minded.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Fever, diaphoresis, and lightheadedness during the hospitalization, now resolved. She feels back to normal.
Neurologic: Headache and spasms before admission. Denies current pain or discomfort.
Gastrointestinal: Significant constipation and vomiting before admission. Now improved after a large bowel movement.
Cardiovascular: Labile blood pressure during the illness.
Otherwise doing well per the patient.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Lungs/chest: The doctor listened to the patient while she took deep breaths and breathed normally. No findings were stated.

RESULTS
Per the hospital course reviewed by the doctor: WBC 23,000 in the ED. Urine cultures were not very impressive. Imaging was an x-ray only, with no CT scan. Her WBC is sometimes mildly elevated at baseline, and last year it was normal.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Acute to chronic constipation, with leukocytosis and recent hospitalization
- The patient believes the hospitalization was more likely due to autonomic dysreflexia from her quadriplegia, triggered by constipation, with significant blood pressure fluctuations. She feels it was less likely a true UTI.
- Urine cultures were unimpressive. Leukocytosis may be related to inflammation or being backed up. Dehydration from the heat may have worsened constipation.
- She has a good bowel regimen: Miralax regularly as primary treatment, and lactulose as rescue for severe constipation.
- Repeat labs in 2 to 3 weeks (the doctor also said 3 to 4 weeks): fasting labs with a CBC to confirm the white count trends down, plus a full cholesterol panel since she is due. If the white count remains elevated, a further bowel-related cause will be considered.
- Counseled on hydration.
- Follow up in 2 to 3 weeks.

2. Quadriplegia
- No specific plan was discussed beyond the above.

3. COVID-19 vaccine status
- She is unvaccinated and hesitant. We had a good discussion.
- The doctor recommended vaccination and considers her high risk because of her quadriplegia. The doctor believes the vaccine is safe, noting rare side effects such as Guillain-Barré, and that vaccination is the only true preventive mechanism. Supplements are not believed to help prevent COVID-19. The doctor is also not convinced that alternative approaches or monoclonal antibodies would help.
- The patient does not want to get COVID but needs to make her own decision. She is somewhat homeopathic. She will think about it and call with questions.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
New right eye twitch.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Karen Nelson is a 3-year-old female with no significant past medical history who presents with her father for evaluation of a new right eye twitch. Her father first noticed it a couple of weeks ago and discussed it with her pediatrician, who referred her for evaluation. The twitch has been noticed every day for the last several weeks. Frequency varies: some days several times an hour, and other days not until late afternoon. When it occurs, the whole side of her face moves for several seconds and then stops, and she appears to blink frequently. Only the face is involved; no other body parts move or twitch. Karen reports it does not hurt. She sometimes feels an urge to move her face, and after it moves she feels better. When it occurs, she continues whatever activity she was doing and does not seem bothered. Her father reports she has otherwise been acting normally, eating well, playing with friends, and going about normal activities. She plays soccer on Saturdays. Her father made a video of the twitch to show the physician. No history of seizures in Karen. No family history of seizures or Tourette syndrome.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: No fever or chills.
Respiratory: No cough.
Neurological: No headache. No seizures. No sleep problems.
Eyes/Face: Facial twitching with frequent blinking as per HPI. No pain.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Neurological: Awake, alert, and oriented x3. Speech is clear and fluent. Gait is steady, and heel-toe walking is normal. Cranial nerves are intact without focal neurologic findings. Able to follow finger with eyes. No pronator drift. Sensation is intact to touch. Reflexes are 2+ and symmetric at the biceps, triceps, knees, and ankles.

RESULTS
Not discussed. (The father's home video of the twitch was mentioned, but no review of it was documented.)

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Tic (eye tic), likely transient tic disorder.
- Tics are common in children, brief, sudden, involuntary motor movements. They typically occur around 5 to 10 years of age and most resolve on their own within a year.
- The movement involves the same part of the body each time, and Karen reports an urge to blink with relief afterward, which makes seizure unlikely.
- Neurological exam is normal. Karen is doing well overall, and the tic has not affected her school or activities.
- The best management is to ignore the tic. Drawing attention to it can make the child self-conscious and worsen it. It may wax and wane and may be more noticeable when she is tired or stressed.
- No medication or other treatment at this time. Treatment can be considered if the tic worsens.
- The father's questions were answered and he agreed with the plan.

Virginia is a patient who injured her right knee 7 days ago while playing basketball when another player ran into her. She fell to the ground, landing on her side, and was unable to continue playing. She reports pain on the inside of the knee. She did not hear or feel a pop. She treated the knee with ice and an Ace wrap and is currently doing exercises, icing, and taking Motrin for pain. She has a history of diabetes, takes metformin 500 mg twice daily, and checks her blood sugars every morning at home. She plays basketball recreationally at the Y.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Musculoskeletal: Right medial knee pain and swelling. No pop felt at the time of injury.
Other systems: Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Right knee:
- Ecchymosis and swelling over the medial aspect.
- Effusion present, which could be fluid or blood.
- Pain to palpation over the medial aspect. No pain with palpation of the lateral aspect.
- Decreased range of motion with flexion and extension. Pain with hyperextension.
- Varus and valgus stress tests negative.

RESULTS
Right knee x-ray (done in office this morning): Bony alignment in good position. No evidence of fracture. Small effusion around the right knee.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Right knee medial collateral ligament strain, possibly from a twisting motion before the fall.
- Continue Ace wrap.
- Right knee brace to be worn for a few days.
- Referral to physical therapy for strengthening of the muscles around the right knee.
- Stop Motrin/Advil and other NSAIDs. Start meloxicam 15 mg daily for pain and swelling.
- Continue exercising with the brace on. Light walking is encouraged.
- No basketball for at least the next 7 days.
- Follow up in 7 days to reassess swelling. If it has worsened or there is concern for significant ligament damage, consider CT or MRI of the knee.

- Concern that reduced activity from the knee injury may affect glycemic control.
- Continue taking metformin and checking blood sugars daily.
- Follow up with PCP, and contact the PCP if blood sugars rise significantly with decreased activity.

Lungs: Auscultated, sounds good.

Left shoulder pain.

Mrs. Anderson is a 44-year-old female presenting with left shoulder pain for one week. Onset followed a gymnastics class, where she may have fallen into an awkward position during a certain move. She feels she overdid it and wonders whether she has a torn rotator cuff. She took Tylenol for two to three days without relief. She reports that any movement of the left shoulder hurts. REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Musculoskeletal: Left shoulder pain with all movement.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Acne on the face.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Kayla Ward is a 7th grade girl (DOB 4/28/07, MRN 384920) seen with her mother as a new patient for acne on the face. The acne started about two years ago and is present most days. She has used over-the-counter washes and Persa-Gel, which have helped a little. There is no itching, bleeding, or pain. The chest and back are not bad. Her current routine: in the morning she wipes her face with water and a washcloth, and occasionally uses an e.l.f. cleanser if she feels greasy. At night she uses the e.l.f. Super Clarity cleanser, then a toner, then Persa-Gel. Today is a good day for her skin. The acne does not flare with her periods. Her periods have been regular for about 2 years. Her mother reports the biggest flare was when she started school sports in the fall, with sweating. Her mother notes Kayla has been diligent with facial care, but it has not helped as much as hoped.

Past medical history: none additional.
Social history: lives with her parents and sister. Pets include a dog, bird, and bunnies. She plays basketball, volleyball, and tap. She wears SPF 30 sunscreen in the summer.
Family history: no additional.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Skin: acne on the face as above; no itching, bleeding, or pain. Chest and back not significantly affected.
Other systems not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Full skin exam performed, except under the underwear and bra.
Skin: Multiple benign nevi on the trunk and extremities. Scattered skin-colored papules. Open and closed comedones and erythematous papules on the face, primarily on the forehead, with some on the central cheeks and chin. Chest and back relatively spared. The remainder of the examination is normal.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Acne vulgaris, mild to moderate, mostly comedonal with a small inflammatory component. (The doctor also mentioned early in the visit that it could be rosacea, but the final assessment was acne.)
- Start topical therapy.
- Morning: wash face with a mild cleanser, then apply a noncomedogenic moisturizer with SPF 30 or higher.
- Evening: wash face with the same cleanser and let it dry. Apply adapalene 0.1% cream in a thin layer to areas that usually break out. Start a few nights a week and work up to nightly. If it is expensive or not covered by insurance, an over-the-counter adapalene gel can be tried. Follow with Clean & Clear Persa-Gel in a thin layer where acne usually occurs, then a noncomedogenic moisturizer.
- Counseled that the topical retinoid may cause sensitivity, dryness, or irritation. Wear sunscreen outdoors.

2. Multiple benign nevi on the arms, legs, back, and abdomen. No worrisome features. Reassurance given.

Follow up in 6 months to assess progress. The family should call the office with any questions or concerns before then.

Left shoulder and left elbow pain for five months following a fall.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Jose James is a new patient with a date of birth of 9/29/1957. He reports constant pain in the left shoulder and left elbow for about five months, which is sometimes severe. The pain began after he slipped on ice while going up a flight of stairs to his house and fell on his left side. He feels his shoulder and wrist took the brunt of the fall. He wonders whether he has a pinched nerve.

The pain is worse with lifting. He has lifted weights two days a week for years and has been unable to lift more than 15 to 20 pounds. Over the past one to two weeks, he has stopped going to the gym because of the pain. He still walks about 30 minutes almost every day with his wife, as he has since retiring from an office job last year.

He has iced the area and stopped exercising, which helped somewhat, but the pain is still bothersome. He has not taken any medication for the pain. He denies numbness or tingling.

Neurological: Denies numbness or tingling.
Musculoskeletal: Positive for left shoulder and left elbow pain, as per HPI.

- No warmth, erythema, or deformity.
- Positive Hawkins-Kennedy and Neer's tests.
- Normal proximal and distal upper extremity strength.
- Median, radial, and ulnar sensation intact.
- Abduction to 90 degrees intact.
- Normal empty can test.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Impingement syndrome of the left shoulder. The doctor does not believe there is an additional injury or issue with the wrist. The wrist pain is attributed to the shoulder. This is a common problem after a fall.

Plan:
1. Physical therapy referral placed for Dr. Martha Rivera, two sessions per week, plus home exercises provided by therapy. The patient will be called within one to two days to schedule.
2. If pain does not improve with therapy, consider a cortisone injection. The patient is not opposed but prefers to try therapy first.
3. Continue icing, especially the shoulder, and rest as much as possible.
4. Call or email if symptoms worsen or do not improve with therapy.

He sleeps with two pillows, which is his baseline, and reports no sleep difficulties. He denies leg swelling and says he has always had thin ankles.

He reports taking his medications as prescribed since discharge and says cost is not a problem because of good insurance. He understands the need to take them continuously to keep his stent open. He was told in the hospital that his heart pump is reduced and that he may retain fluid. He was advised to limit salt and acknowledges that this will be difficult because he likes pizza.

Neck: No jugular venous distention. No carotid bruits.
Cardiac: 3/6 systolic ejection murmur heard at the left base, similar to last year.

- Labs next week.

Tobacco: He is a former smoker, at least 2 packs per day for 20+ years, and quit about 4 years ago.

Constitutional: No fever or chills.
Cardiovascular: No chest pain. No calf pain with walking.

Not discussed. The patient reports a prior hemoglobin A1c above 9, but no result was reviewed.

Nonhealing foot ulcer.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Gregory presents with a nonhealing foot ulcer that he has had for about two months. It has recently become red and is draining, which is new for him and is his main concern. He thinks he may have gotten it from walking barefoot on the beach (Dewey Beach). He has no specific pain, but it sometimes throbs. His PCP prescribed an antibiotic, but he has not yet picked it up from the pharmacy. He does not recall the name, but says he has taken it before. He has diabetes and takes his medication, but he does not check his blood sugar regularly and is not sure how. He believes his last A1c was around 10. His PCP mentioned that this office might provide a surgical shoe, and he does not currently have one.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: No fever reported.
Musculoskeletal/Skin: Foot ulcer with new redness and drainage, as in the HPI. Intermittent throbbing, no specific pain.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Normal. Afebrile.
Right foot: One by two inch circular wound on the dorsal aspect of the lateral right foot, just proximal to the fifth MTP joint. Redness, drainage, and edema around the wound, with fluid draining from it. No necrosis, no odor, and no bony exposure. On palpation, the patient feels increased pressure but not distinct pain.

RESULTS
X-ray of the right foot: No evidence of osteomyelitis.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Diabetic foot ulcer, right lateral foot, with soft tissue infection. There is no osteomyelitis on x-ray, and the infection appears limited to the skin.
- Order ankle brachial index (ABI) to assess blood supply and healing potential.
- Debridement of devitalized tissue performed in the office today.
- Start clindamycin 400 mg twice daily for 7 days.
- Provide a surgical shoe to wear for the next month to offload pressure.
- Follow up in 2 weeks, with possible repeat debridement at that time.

2. Diabetes, poorly controlled (patient-reported A1c about 10). This is likely contributing to the poor wound healing.
- Return to the PCP for a treatment plan to control blood sugar.

Return precautions: Call the office if any issues arise in the meantime. Go to urgent care or the ER for emergencies, such as fever, feeling unwell, or the foot turning black.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Follow-up for rheumatoid arthritis. Persistent right knee swelling and pain, now with swelling of the whole leg.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Tyler Nelson is a male with DOB 3/6/1949 (MRN 385729) who presents for ongoing management of rheumatoid arthritis. At his last visit he received a steroid injection in the right knee. It helped for about a couple of weeks. Since then the knee has remained swollen and painful, and for roughly two months the swelling has progressed to involve the whole leg. Pain is currently 3/10 and is typically 6/10 on a normal day. He wears compression socks much of the time, which help somewhat, but swelling persists, especially around the knee. He has slowed down some in daily activities. Pain is worst after prolonged sitting; he is very stiff on first standing and uses a cane to steady himself, and the stiffness loosens after a short time. He reports taking Xeljanz XR (he believes 11 mg daily) every day. He also started Celebrex 200 mg daily about 2 months ago, which worked well until the swelling recurred. He reports eating a lot of salty snacks. He has not discussed the swelling with his primary care doctor. He previously had physical therapy for the other knee some years ago.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Musculoskeletal: Right knee pain, swelling, and stiffness on standing; leg swelling.
Other systems: Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Right knee/leg: Range of motion slightly diminished; pain with full extension. Pitting edema around the knee and ankle. Normal capillary refill in the toes. Knee is warm to palpation. Patient describes soreness on palpation, like an old bruise.

RESULTS
Per physician, CMP levels are good this visit. No imaging results available.

Procedure: Right knee fluid aspiration and steroid injection. Risks, benefits, and alternatives were explained, including risks of hypopigmentation, soft tissue atrophy, tendon rupture, and transient hypoglycemia. Verbal consent obtained. The right knee was prepped in standard fashion and accessed via the lateral approach. 3 mL of initially clear, then blood-tinged fluid was aspirated. The knee was injected with 80 mg triamcinolone and 1 mL lidocaine. Tolerated well with no complications. Post-procedure instructions given.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Rheumatoid arthritis with right knee pain, swelling, and warmth suggesting inflammation. Physician raised possible gout, uncertain.
- Right knee aspiration and steroid injection (triamcinolone 80 mg with lidocaine) performed today.
- X-ray of the right knee ordered to evaluate the cause of swelling.
- Refer to physical therapy.
- Surgical consult if no improvement.
- Continue Xeljanz XR and Celebrex 200 mg daily.

2. Leg edema, right.
- X-ray to look for cause.
- Continue compression socks, reduce salt intake, and elevate feet when possible, especially at night.
- If no improvement, make an appointment with primary care physician.

3. Medication monitoring (Xeljanz, high-risk medication).
- CMP is checked every couple of months. Levels are good currently. Patient to schedule blood work before next visit.

Patient will follow up with his PCP.

Shortness of breath.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Rachel is a 48-year-old female with a history of depression, smoking, and chronic back pain who presents for shortness of breath. She reports that with very mild exercise or just walking, such as walking up her driveway, she has palpitations and a little shortness of breath. This has been happening more often lately. She is unsure whether it is related to her back pain. She has been exercising more recently to lose weight gained during COVID. 

Smoking: At her last visit she was smoking two packs per day. She has cut down significantly and now smokes about one cigarette once a day.

Depression: She has "moments." Some days she wakes up and everything is great, and other days she feels extremely low. She is unsure what triggers this, possibly the weather. She is still taking Effexor.

Chronic back pain: She takes gabapentin (Neurontin), which she feels helps and she feels better, but the pain still comes on every now and then. When it is bad, she rests as much as she can. She has not made yoga a habit.

She reports no other issues or concerns.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Review of systems was done by the nurse and not detailed in this transcript.
Respiratory: Positive for shortness of breath with mild exertion.
Cardiovascular: Positive for palpitations with mild exertion.
Musculoskeletal: Positive for intermittent chronic back pain.
Psychiatric: Positive for intermittent low mood.
Patient reports no other issues.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Physical exam is largely normal except for mild wheezes in all lung fields.

RESULTS
Pulmonary function tests: Suggest possible asthma or COPD.
Chest x-ray: Diaphragm is somewhat flattened, which can be seen in COPD, often in smokers.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease)
- Diagnosed based on pulmonary function tests, chest x-ray, and exam findings with mild diffuse wheezes. Explained that this means she cannot exhale appropriately.
- Start Combivent inhaler, two puffs twice a day.
- Prescribe albuterol, two puffs as needed for significant shortness of breath (rescue inhaler).
- Prescribe prednisone taper pack.
- Noted significant reduction in smoking, now about one cigarette daily; praised progress.

2. Depression
- Stable. Continue Effexor with no changes.
- Yoga was recommended.

3. Chronic back pain
- Continue gabapentin (Neurontin) with no changes.
- Yoga was recommended.

The patient had no questions and agreed with the plan.

He has a history of diabetes and has not been seen for follow-up in some time. He reports feeling okay and takes his medications. He is on metformin twice a day. He tries to check his blood sugar most mornings but sometimes misses it. He reports recent readings have trended on the higher side. He exercises when he gets the chance. His family owns a bakery, and he reports that he visits and ends up eating some of the products, though he says it is not much and he tries to limit it.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Musculoskeletal: Positive for low back pain, worse with sudden twisting to the left.
Neurological: Negative for numbness or tingling in the feet.

No results available. The last A1c was almost five months ago, and the value was not discussed.

- Continue diet and exercise.

- Medication adjustments will be reviewed once A1c results are available.

Brittany Edwards is a 32-year-old female last seen in August 2019 for flares of abdominal pain. She was diagnosed with IBS and treated with Bentyl. She had a previous prescription for Reglan from the emergency room, used as needed for nausea. At that visit she was instructed to start a daily low-dose fiber supplement such as Citrucel, probiotics for gas and bloating, Bentyl up to four times daily for intestinal cramping, and to stop Reglan and use Zofran as needed. Neuromodulators such as Elavil and BuSpar were discussed but not started.

Today she reports she has not been feeling well. She has been going out to eat on Friday and Saturday nights and has had spicy foods, including spicy shrimp. She reports both lower abdominal symptoms (cramping) and upper symptoms (nausea). She wonders whether she has lactose intolerance. On normal days she has 2-3 formed bowel movements per day. She tends to have more diarrhea after going out and drinking with friends. At Friday's restaurant she usually eats chicken alfredo pasta, which she says normally does not bother her. She usually drinks tequila (prefers Patron) or dark liquor, limiting herself to two brown liquor drinks, and occasionally a martini. She has not had luck using fiber such as Citrucel regularly. During the week she is still having cramping and sharp pains and has been avoiding heavy foods. She had fried chicken today and was fine for the most part. She has noticed doing better drinking water rather than sodas. She is interested in a daily medication to help avoid flares altogether.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Gastrointestinal: Positive for diarrhea, nausea, and abdominal pain (cramping and sharp pains).

General: Alert and cooperative, appears stated age.
Lungs: Clear to auscultation bilaterally.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm.
Abdomen: Soft, non-tender. No masses or organomegaly. Normal active bowel sounds. Patient denies tenderness.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Brittany Edwards is a pleasant female with IBS and functional abdominal pain, aggravated by high stress, poor eating habits, and poor sleeping habits.

1. IBS with functional abdominal pain:
- Encouraged dietary and lifestyle modifications.
- Start Elavil (neuromodulator) 25 mg every night at bedtime for IBS. Counseled that it may cause some sleepiness.
- Citrucel tablets twice daily for regularity.
- Bentyl 20 mg as needed: one tablet 30 to 45 minutes before leaving the house when going out to eat, with a second tablet at the restaurant, repeat up to four times daily. No need to use it on days she feels well. Refill sent.

- Try to identify patterns in foods and drinks that worsen symptoms.
- Reduce greasy and fatty foods, sugary drinks, and alcohol. Continue drinking plenty of water.
- Zofran may be used if needed, but not taken ahead of time.
3. Prescriptions sent to her pharmacy.
4. Follow-up in one month via MyChart email regarding symptoms, side effects or issues with Elavil, and whether adjustments are needed.

Right elbow pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Teresa presents with right medial elbow pain that has lasted about four days. The pain radiates down the medial aspect of her arm. She does not recall hitting the elbow and has no prior elbow injury. She has been doing a lot of pottery on a wheel, working on a ceramic bowl for her son's birthday, and cannot work on it now because of the pain. She rates the pain at 7/10 at its worst. It wakes her at night when she rolls over. Ibuprofen has not helped, and she tried a little ice at first. The pain is not getting better.

Hypertension: She is on lisinopril 10 mg and takes it daily with an alarm. Home blood pressures run in the 110s to 130s.

Diabetes: She is on metformin 500 mg twice daily. She sometimes forgets doses because she is out and about. She admits to a sweet tooth and bakes cakes and cinnamon rolls, and she tastes them. Home sugars are sometimes 150 to 170. She had a diabetic consult a long time ago and is open to seeing a dietitian again.

Exercise: She walks in the morning and evening, about 1 to 2 miles daily.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Musculoskeletal: Right medial elbow pain radiating down the medial arm, as above.
Sleep: Pain disrupts sleep.
Skin: No rash, bruising, or swelling noted at the elbow (per exam).
Other systems: Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: BP 120/70. Respiratory rate 18. Temperature 97.9. Oxygen saturation 100%. Pulse appropriate. Pain 7/10. Weight is up about 5 pounds from the last visit.
Cardiovascular: No murmur, rub, or gallop. Pulses equal bilaterally.
Respiratory: Lungs clear to auscultation bilaterally.
Skin/Elbow: No rash, bruising, swelling, discoloration, or lesions at the elbow.
Musculoskeletal (right elbow): Moderate tenderness at the medial epicondyle. Pain with resisted pronation of the right forearm. Pain with wrist flexion. No pain with supination (turning the wrist outward, as with opening a doorknob).

RESULTS
Right elbow x-ray: No fracture or bony abnormality.
A1c: Ordered, pending.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Right medial epicondylitis (overuse tendon injury). The x-ray shows no fracture or bony abnormality, which supports a tendon-related cause.
- Rest the arm and wear a sling while awake. A sling is ordered.
- Ice the elbow for 20 minutes three times daily.
- Ibuprofen 600 mg (3 pills) every 6 hours with food for one week.
- Hold pottery for the next couple of weeks.
- Consider physical rehab if healing is slow. This will be discussed at the next visit.

2. Type 2 diabetes, longstanding, with suboptimal control and inconsistent adherence.
- Increase metformin to 1000 mg twice daily.
- Check and record blood sugars daily.
- Order A1c.
- Refer to diabetic counseling/dietitian. Advised to cut back on taste-testing baked goods.
- Follow up in a couple of weeks. Other medication options will be evaluated if sugars remain uncontrolled.

Emergency room follow-up for chest pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Roger is a 62-year-old male seen for follow-up after an ER visit for chest discomfort. Over the weekend he was doing yard work in hot weather and developed shortness of breath and chest pain lasting about an hour. He has never had this before. He felt fine after he finished the yard work and has had no further symptoms since. He was kept in the ER for a few hours, and his blood pressure, which was about 180/95 on arrival, seemed to regulate. His blood pressure usually does not run this high. He has a history of hypertension and takes lisinopril 10 mg daily. He had knee surgery a couple of months ago and has had no problems with rehab and recovery. He has had no chest pain during physical therapy exercises. No immediate family history of heart disease; a cousin has heart disease.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Cardiovascular: Chest pain during the episode, none since.
Respiratory: Shortness of breath during the episode, none since.
No other symptoms since the episode.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Neck: Mildly enlarged thyroid, non-tender. Right carotid bruit.
Lungs: Clear.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm. 3/6 systolic ejection murmur.
Abdomen: Soft.
Musculoskeletal/Extremities: Healed scar on right knee from prior surgery. No lower extremity edema.

RESULTS
Blood pressure: Still elevated today (ER reading about 180/95).
EKG: Normal.
Echocardiogram: Mildly reduced cardiac pumping function.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
62-year-old male with an episode of chest pain that could be related to severe hypertension or to underlying heart disease. Echocardiogram shows reduced pumping function, which needs further evaluation. EKG is normal. Blood pressure remains elevated.
1. Chest pain: Order cardiac catheterization to evaluate for blockages in the coronary arteries. The nurse will schedule it.
2. Hypertension: Start carvedilol 25 mg twice daily, which also helps with coronary disease and pumping function. Continue lisinopril 10 mg daily. Reassess blood pressure on this regimen.
3. Reduced cardiac pumping function: Further evaluation to follow.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Right knee pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Rebecca is a 27-year-old female with a history of carpal tunnel release a couple of years ago, chronic back pain, and depression. She presents with right knee pain. Over the past month she has taken up swimming more regularly to be more active. Last week she began to have significant right knee pain. The pain occurs only while swimming and only in the right knee. She swims breaststroke, with a frog-like kick. A month ago she could swim ten laps, but now the pain starts after a couple of laps. She does not recall any fall, twist, or other injury.

Chronic back pain: comes and goes, currently doing very well. No pain radiating down the legs.

Depression: doing very well on medication, therapy, and spending more time outdoors. Sleeping and eating well. No thoughts of harming herself or others.

Carpal tunnel: doing very well since release. She has full range of motion and feels much better. No flare-ups.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Per nurse's review of systems before the visit, no significant issues.
Musculoskeletal: Right knee pain with swimming. Chronic back pain currently well controlled, without radiation to the legs.
Psychiatric: Depression stable. No suicidal or homicidal ideation. Sleeping and eating well.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Cardiovascular: Heart regular.
Respiratory: Lungs clear.
Neck: Thyroid normal. No adenopathy.
Musculoskeletal: No swelling of the knee joint. Mild pain with range of motion of the right knee. Significant pain with patellar manipulation/inhibition testing, which reproduced most of her pain. Grip strength equal bilaterally.
Other: Remainder of exam essentially normal.

RESULTS
Right knee x-ray: Normal.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Chondromalacia of the right patella, due to overuse from swimming.
- Ibuprofen 600 mg four times a day with food.
- Straight leg raising exercises to strengthen the quadriceps.
- Avoid activities that put extra pressure on the knees, including lunges and breaststroke. She may swim other strokes with straight knees or take a break from swimming.
- Follow up if not improving in a couple of weeks.

2. Chronic back pain: well controlled. She may continue swimming after the knee improves. Call if it flares up.

3. Depression: stable. Continue current medication with no changes.

4. Carpal tunnel, status post release: stable. No changes.

Shortness of breath.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Alan is a 61-year-old male who presents with shortness of breath. Over the weekend he took a very long bike ride of about three hours. When he got back he was very lightheaded and short of breath. This surprised him because he bikes every morning and has never had this problem before. He reports it was hard to catch his breath afterward and that he may have had a little chest pain, which resolved after about an hour. He had a mild cough with his first cold in the last year and a half, which resolved after about a week. No sick contacts in the family. He denies nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain.

Migraines: under control with Imitrex and avoidance of bright lights. He is still taking Imitrex.
Reflux: managing well on Protonix.
Cataract surgery: about four and a half months ago. His vision has been great since.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Fever was asked about; the patient's answer was cut off and not clearly given.
Cardiovascular: Possible mild chest pain after the bike ride, resolved after about an hour.
Respiratory: Shortness of breath after exertion. Cough with a cold, resolved.
Gastrointestinal: No nausea, vomiting, or abdominal pain.
Neurological: Lightheadedness after the bike ride.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Reviewed; doctor reports everything looks quite good, with perfect oxygenation.
Neck: Supple. No jugular venous distension.
Cardiovascular: Regular rhythm. No murmur.
Respiratory: Slight expiratory wheeze bilaterally, heard with every breath.
Extremities: Trace lower extremity edema.

RESULTS

- Pulmonary referral ordered.
- Follow up in a couple of weeks.
- Call right away if shortness of breath recurs.

3. Reflux: Stable. Continue Protonix.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Abdominal pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Karen is a 34-year-old female with a history of chronic migraines and hypertension who presents with abdominal pain.

The pain began about 10 days ago as mild right-sided discomfort and has worsened over the last couple of days. It waxes and wanes, generally 4-5 out of 10, sometimes reaching 7-8 out of 10. It is usually worse after meals and is not too bad in the morning before eating. It is mostly localized to the right side and may radiate slightly to the left. It is tender to palpation, and certain positions worsen it when the pain is at its highest. She reports nausea and a little heartburn but no vomiting. She has had no urinary symptoms and no change in bowel habits, with no diarrhea or blood in the stool. Appetite is decreased because of the nausea, and she has felt more fatigued over the past week. She has had chills but no documented fevers. She has not eaten anything unusual, has had no recent travel other than within Wisconsin, and has had no unusual exposures.

Migraines: Episodes have been rare, and none recently. She treats them with Excedrin Migraine and uses sumatriptan if there is no response to the over-the-counter analgesic. She needs a refill of sumatriptan.

Hypertension: She takes lisinopril 20 mg daily and checks her blood pressure about 2-3 times a week rather than daily. Readings are usually systolic in the 120s to low 130s and diastolic in the 70s. She is running low on lisinopril and requests a refill.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Positive for fatigue over the past week and chills. No documented fevers.
GI: Positive for abdominal pain, nausea, heartburn, and decreased appetite. No vomiting, diarrhea, or blood in stool.
GU: No dysuria or hematuria.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Cardiovascular: Grade 3/6 systolic ejection murmur, unchanged from prior exam. Otherwise normal cardiovascular exam.
Abdomen: Mild to moderate right upper quadrant tenderness. Equivocal Murphy's sign in the right upper quadrant (pain with deep breath on palpation). Remainder of abdomen soft without significant tenderness. No right lower quadrant tenderness with deep palpation.
Back: No CVA tenderness.
Other: Remainder of exam normal and unremarkable. Blood pressure noted by the physician to be a little elevated today. She is afebrile.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Acute abdominal pain with right upper quadrant tenderness. Concern for gallstones or possible gallbladder infection.
- Order CBC, chem 12, urinalysis, pregnancy test, and right upper quadrant ultrasound today.
- Patient to remain in clinic while testing is done.
- Send to the emergency department if results warrant.
- NPO for now in case surgery is needed, which is unlikely but possible.
- Physician will follow up on results before the patient leaves, with the hope that she can go home today.

2. Chronic migraines. Occasional episodes, none recent.
- Continue Excedrin as needed.
- Continue sumatriptan as needed for breakthrough migraine, and refill sumatriptan.
- Continue to avoid alcohol and caffeine binges and get enough sleep.

3. Hypertension. Appears adequately controlled.
- Continue lisinopril 20 mg daily, and send a refill to the pharmacy.
- Encouraged to check blood pressure daily.

Follow-up in about 4 weeks.

Routine follow-up of chronic medical conditions. The patient also raised increased fatigue, pursed lip breathing, and a right testicular/epididymal nodule.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Mr. Walker is a 61-year-old male (DOB 4/14/1960) presenting for routine follow-up of chronic medical conditions. He underwent aortic valve replacement and ascending aortic aneurysm repair in January 2013. (The date was stated as 1/22/2013 at the start of the visit and 1/20/2013 in the assessment.)

He reports increased fatigue and is unsure whether it is due to age or to being drained at the end of the day. He still rides a road bike, typically 20 to 30 miles, and says it is early in the season. In prior years he could ride 40 miles on a good day. He cannot go as fast as he used to, and his riding partner now waits for him. After a long ride he sits down and is "out," and he needs a break when he gets home. He states nothing has changed drastically since his last visit. He denies that the tiredness is depression and describes himself as a happy person.

He is eight years out from his valve surgery and was told at the time that the valve would last about eight years. He wants to confirm that the valve is holding up and has asked Dr. Lewis for an echocardiogram. His last stress test was 9/9/2019. He no longer follows up at Hopkins because it is too stressful, and he gets intermittent follow-up here.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Right index finger pain and stiffness after a motor vehicle accident; seeking a second opinion.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Philip Gutierrez is a 50-year-old right-handed male (DOB 1/12/71) who works as an x-ray tech. He presents for a second opinion regarding his right index finger. In March of this year (about 3 months ago) he was a passenger in a car that was rear-ended multiple times. He felt two bumps that slung him forward and caused him to stretch out his right index finger. He felt as though he laid on the finger and it went backward, consistent with a hyperextension injury. He thinks it might be dislocated. The finger has hurt and remained swollen since the accident. He cannot make a fist, the pain is sometimes unbearable, and even driving hurts.

He has been seen at an outside orthopedic practice, largely by the physical therapy/occupational therapy staff and a PA, and has done therapy there. An MRI was obtained for concern about capsular strain with or without rupture of the FDS tendon. He reports being told he has a tear in the finger and that an injection would worsen the tear. He then understood that the orthopedist would not do surgery but would do an injection, and he is confused by the conflicting messages. He was previously offered an injection but declined steroid because of a reaction to dexamethasone that makes his heart race. He was scheduled to see Dr. Alice Davis, but it does not appear he did. Occupational therapy tried maneuvers to straighten the finger, but it hurt afterward and the whole finger swelled. He bought a splint himself, thinking it would straighten the finger. He feels he is not getting medical care and came to see if anything can be done, as he needs his right hand.

No diabetes or rheumatoid arthritis. He takes a blood pressure pill and no other chronic medications.
Allergies/reactions: dexamethasone (heart racing), methylprednisolone (itching).

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Musculoskeletal: right index finger pain, swelling, and stiffness; unable to make a fist.
Neurologic: slight numbness in the finger with palpation on exam.
Other systems not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
General: Very pleasant, cooperative, healthy male in no distress.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm. 2+ radial pulse.
Right hand: No swelling or bruising in the palm or over the volar surface of the index finger. Normal creases, slightly diminished over the PIP of the index finger compared to the middle finger. The index finger rests in about 10 degrees of PIP flexion. Pressing on the volar index finger is uncomfortable; at an adjacent site it is not. The patient reports the finger feels a little numb. Attempted flexion of the fingertip and the finger caused a sensation of tearing. Passive bending at the MCP joint was painful. The pain appears to be stretching-related from lack of motion. Extensor tendons and collateral ligaments are intact.

RESULTS
MRI right index finger (4/24/2021, outside facility): focal soft tissue swelling over the right index MCP joint; partial-thickness tear of the right FDS; fluid consistent with tenosynovitis around the FDP and FDS tendons. Radial and ulnar collateral ligaments of the index MCP joint intact, as is the MCP joint capsule. Extensor tendons intact.

X-ray right hand, 4 views (today): no bony abnormalities, joint congruency throughout all lesser digits, no concerning soft tissue shadows, no arthritis.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Post-traumatic, rather severe stenosing tenosynovitis of the right index finger, with a partial tear of one half of the FDS tendon.
- The FDS is the less important of the two flexor tendons, and the FDP, which goes to the fingertip, is intact. Scar tissue and inflammation around the FDS are likely blocking excursion of the other tendons through the pulley. The finger is stiff and sore, with intact collateral ligaments and extensors.
- Steroid injection: the plan was a trigger finger injection with 1 cc betamethasone (Celestone) and 0.5 cc lidocaine. Dexamethasone is to be avoided given his reaction. Benefit is expected in 3 to 5 days, with further improvement over a couple of weeks, and the injection may need to be repeated.
- Procedure: the first attempt was stopped when the patient had a dramatic, violent painful reaction to needle introduction, with contortions and withdrawal of the hand and concern for a needle stick. The needle was withdrawn. He was counseled on the importance of getting steroid into the flexor tendon sheath. A second attempt with the same technique and doses was made. A small palmar vein bled a scant amount, which was cleaned up and a Band-Aid applied. He was reassured repeatedly that no harm was done to the finger.
- Aftercare: ice this evening and take ibuprofen. It is safe to drive.
- Activity: he needs to start moving the finger actively, which will not tear anything or break a bone. A splint immobilizes the finger and does not help.
- Therapy: outpatient prescription for therapy once a week for 6 weeks, preferably at the same facility as before, for accountability. The goal is full active and passive range of motion without restrictions.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Jacqueline is a patient referred after her PCP's recent blood work indicated hepatitis C. She feels anxious and surprised about the result because she has been feeling fine. She has never previously been told she has hepatitis C. She reports remote IV drug use years ago but has been clean for over fifteen years. No known hepatitis C positive partners were reported.

She reports she tends to be very tired at the end of the day after work. She states work has not been busier than usual, and she feels she is getting enough sleep but still becomes very tired by the end of the day. She notes this is a change from before. She had a physical with her PCP and nothing else was found.

Alcohol: previously drank much more; currently about one beer a day, slightly more on weekends.
Tobacco: current smoker, down to one to two cigarettes a day from a peak of 1.5 packs per day.
No other medical conditions reported.
Family history: hypertension, diabetes, and depression.
Social: married with children. Describes herself as a workaholic but is working on it.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Positive for fatigue at the end of the day. Otherwise feels well.
Other systems not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Reviewed by physician and reported as good.
General: No distress.
Skin: No jaundice.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm. 2/6 systolic murmur, unchanged from last year.
Respiratory: Lungs clear with no wheezes, rales, or rhonchi.
Abdomen: Bowel sounds present. Soft. No splenomegaly appreciated.
Musculoskeletal: No gait disturbance. No edema.

RESULTS
HCV antibody: positive.
Liver panel: AST elevated at 39. ALT, albumin, and total bilirubin within normal limits.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Hepatitis C
Initial labs are consistent with hepatitis C, a viral infection of the liver. She has likely had it for years. The physician explained this to the patient.
- Confirm diagnosis with HCV RNA and HCV genotype.
- Order a special ultrasound to assess for liver fibrosis and determine severity of liver disease.
- Treatment to be determined based on these results.
- Family screening: the patient asked about her wife and children. They should undergo the same screening she had. She will have them make appointments with their family doctor.

2. Systolic murmur
- 2/6, unchanged from last year. Continue to monitor.

3. Tobacco use
- Acknowledged reduction in smoking and encouraged her to keep it up.

Follow-up: Nurse to schedule testing. Return visit in about three weeks.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Left knee pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Angela is a patient who presents with left knee pain that began about one week ago. She fell and twisted her knee while running around with her niece, who is learning to ride a bike without training wheels. She heard a pop when she twisted it. She has been limping since the injury and reports no improvement. The pain is on both sides of the knee, worse on the medial side than the lateral side. Pain started at about 4/10 and is getting worse. It is now throbbing. She has a recent history of an ulcer, and her doctor told her not to take NSAIDs such as Advil or ibuprofen. She has been taking Tylenol, which helps only a little, and the pain returns within 1 to 2 hours. She has also wrapped the knee with kinesiology tape.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Musculoskeletal: Left knee pain and limping as per HPI.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Left knee: Edema present. Effusion present. Moderate range of motion, able to move the knee but not through full range. Pain on flexion and extension. Tenderness to palpation over the medial knee. Lachman's test negative. Valgus and varus stress tests negative.

RESULTS
X-ray of the left knee: Normal. No fracture or bony abnormality.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Left knee pain, likely medial collateral ligament (MCL) strain. The mechanism was a twisting injury. Exam showed no evidence of ligament tear, and the x-ray was normal. The doctor mentioned meniscus tear early in the visit, but the exam findings do not suggest anything is torn.
- Start tramadol 50 mg twice daily as a non-NSAID pain medication, given her history of ulcer.
- Continue Tylenol as needed for breakthrough pain, without exceeding the safe dose because of liver risk.
- Knee immobilizer, worn for the next week, to limit movement, allow healing, and reduce inflammation.
- Ice 3 to 4 times a day for 20 to 30 minutes at a time to reduce swelling.
- Avoid running for about 3 weeks.
- Expected return to normal activity in about 1 month.
- If symptoms worsen, she should call the office. She may need further imaging such as an MRI. The doctor asked her to report how she feels in a couple of days.
