Evaluation of kidney stones (referred by PCP).

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Mason is a patient referred by his PCP for evaluation of a kidney stone. About one week ago, while working in the barn moving hay, he developed sudden-onset right back pain. He initially attributed it to throwing hay. He also broke out into a sweat and became nauseated. He saw his PCP, who ordered a CT scan that showed a kidney stone. He has never had a kidney stone before. His father has had kidney stones many times.

The pain radiated almost to the groin but not all the way down. Since the initial episode he has had no more severe pain. After the diagnosis the pain recurred a couple of times but did not last as long. He has been straining his urine as instructed and has not seen anything in the strainer. He denies blood in the urine and denies darker urine.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Sweating at onset of pain, as above.
GI: Nausea at onset of pain.
GU: No hematuria, no darker urine. No stone passage seen in strainer.
Musculoskeletal: Right back pain radiating toward the groin, as above.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: No fever. Blood pressure and heart rate normal.
Abdomen: No tenderness to palpation. No rebound or guarding.
Back: Right CVA tenderness.

RESULTS
CT (reviewed by physician): 0.5 cm stone in the proximal right ureter. No evidence of hydronephrosis.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Right proximal ureteral stone, 0.5 cm, without hydronephrosis. The right CVA tenderness is expected given the stone.
- Push fluids to facilitate passage of the stone.
- Prescribe oxycodone 5 mg every 6 to 8 hours for pain.
- May use Tylenol between oxycodone doses for breakthrough pain.
- Continue straining urine until the stone passes.
- Order BMP, urinalysis, and urine culture. Antibiotics will be prescribed if the urinalysis suggests infection.
- Follow up in 1 to 2 weeks, with the hope that the stone will have passed. If it has not, discuss further treatment such as lithotripsy, a noninvasive shock wave procedure that breaks up the stone.
- The nurse will bring the prescription.

Right shoulder pain for a few weeks. Also bilateral foot and ankle soreness.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Bobby is a patient with right shoulder pain for a few weeks. It began after he did multiple backyard projects, including building an outdoor shower, extending a patio, making flower boxes, and laying stone in flower beds, which involves lifting. He was sore all over for a couple of days afterward, but the right shoulder has stayed sore and has not gone away. He thinks it could be bursitis.

The right shoulder is his dominant side. He injured it playing baseball when he was younger and has had some ongoing minor issues. He does not feel the pain is in the rotator cuff. It is more on the outside of the shoulder and tender there when he raises his arm. He reports no restriction in movement. Pain occurs with movement and not at rest. It bothers him a little at night because he sleeps on that side. He has been taking Advil and icing, which helps a little. The shoulder remains sore to touch, but the medications dull the pain. He denies numbness in the arm or hands.

He also reports soreness and stiffness in both feet and ankle joints after a lot of yard work. His wife thinks he does not drink enough water. He has been elevating and icing his feet with slight improvement. He does not recall a specific injury.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: No fever.
Musculoskeletal: Right shoulder pain with movement and at night. No restriction in arm movement. Bilateral foot and ankle soreness and stiffness.
Neurological: No numbness in the arms or hands.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Temperature 97.8, heart rate 62, respirations 16, blood pressure 116/84, oxygen saturation 99%.
Right shoulder: Limited active and passive range of motion. Tenderness at the greater tuberosity of the humerus. No tenderness at the sternoclavicular or acromioclavicular joints. Good hand grip.
Neurovascular, right arm: Capillary refill less than 3 seconds. Sensation to touch intact.

RESULTS
Right shoulder x-ray: No fracture.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Right shoulder pain, most likely rotator cuff tendinopathy (injury to the tendons of the shoulder muscles).

2. Bilateral foot and ankle soreness, no known injury.
- Try soaking the feet in Epsom salts to help the muscles relax and ease soreness.
- Continue elevation and icing.
- The patient agrees with the plan.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Neck pain following a motor vehicle accident.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Jack is a patient who presents with neck pain that began after a car accident about one week ago. He was hit from behind, and his neck and head were thrown forward quickly. He has had pain ever since. He rates the pain 7/10. It is not constant but occurs whenever he moves his head, which he does often. The pain is located in the back of the neck and does not radiate to the upper back or shoulders. He took ibuprofen, which helped only a little, bringing the pain to about 5/10. The pain has stayed the same overall and worsens with neck movement. He can mostly turn his neck from side to side, but it is painful. He had a couple of headaches early on and reports having had one lately. He did not go to the emergency room because of cost. He is unaware of any swelling or bruising of the neck. He played football years ago and had no neck problems then.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Neurological: Headaches as above. No radiation of pain.
HEENT: No hearing problems or visual disturbances.
Musculoskeletal: Neck pain with movement as above. No known neck swelling.
Skin: No known bruising of the neck.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Neck: Positive pain to palpation of the soft tissues of the neck. Positive pain with flexion. Severe pain with extension. Positive pain with rotation. Positive pain with lateral bending; the patient is unable to touch ear to shoulder.
Back and shoulders: No pain to palpation.

RESULTS
X-ray reviewed: no signs of fracture or bony abnormalities.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Neck strain (whiplash) following a motor vehicle accident, causing neck pain.
- Conservative treatment.
- Motrin 600 mg every 6 to 8 hours.
- Flexeril 10 mg every 12 hours as needed.
- Avoid straining the neck and move conservatively.
- Order MRI because he did not go to the emergency room, to make sure there is no concussion and to evaluate for nerve impingement.
- After MRI results, refer to physical rehab/physical therapy or a chiropractor. The patient voiced reservations about chiropractors, and the doctor said physical therapy or rehab can be considered instead.
- The patient had no further questions.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Lung nodule found incidentally on imaging, referred for evaluation. The patient is nervous about the finding.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Kyle was seen by his PCP for a cough, which was diagnosed as bronchitis. A chest x-ray was done to rule out pneumonia and showed a lung nodule. A follow-up CT scan confirmed the nodule, and he was referred here.

The cough has been present off and on for about three months. He first noticed it more when he spent a day loading hay for his horses, after which the coughing increased. He then developed a cold, which led him to see his PCP. The cough has since resolved. He wonders whether allergies may play a role. He exercises regularly, bikes a lot, and typically does not get sick.

He denies pain and shortness of breath.

History of rheumatoid arthritis: it is fairly controlled. He takes methotrexate, which he thinks is 7.5 mg weekly. His joints feel okay as long as he stays active. Problems occur mostly in his hands, and he has had no recent flares.

Former smoker. He quit about 7 years ago and has remained tobacco free.

Family history: no lung cancer. His mother had breast cancer and is doing well now.

He has no known history of lung infections or pneumonia.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Respiratory: Cough as above, now resolved. No shortness of breath.
Constitutional: No fever noted today.
Musculoskeletal: Intermittent hand joint symptoms related to RA. No recent flares.
Cardiovascular: No pain reported.
Psychiatric: Reports feeling nervous and scared.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: BP 124/76. HR 70. RR 16. O2 saturation 98% on room air. Afebrile.
Lungs: Clear and equal bilaterally to auscultation.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm. No clicks, rubs, or murmurs. No extra beats.
Extremities: Skin pink, warm, and dry. No lower extremity edema. Mild swelling of the knuckles of the third digit on each hand, which can be normal in RA. Pulses intact in all extremities. Capillary refill brisk.

RESULTS
Chest CT: Solitary 2 cm nodule in the lateral aspect of the right upper lobe. The nodule is smooth in appearance. No evidence of emphysematous disease.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Incidentally found right upper lobe lung nodule, 2 cm, smooth, in a former smoker.
- Order pulmonary function tests for a baseline assessment of lung function.
- Schedule a PET CT to determine whether the nodule is metabolically active, which could suggest cancer or inflammation.
- Recommend removal by video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS). This involves three small incisions on the right chest, with removal of the nodule along with a very small portion of lung.
- The procedure is done under general anesthesia and takes about 1.5 hours.
- He will be admitted afterward with a chest tube, which will be removed at bedside the following day. Expected hospital stay is one night.
- The nodule could be benign, but removal is recommended because of his smoking history.
- Paperwork to be signed to start the treatment process. The patient had no questions. He expressed fear, and the doctor offered reassurance and support.

2. Rheumatoid arthritis.
- Continue methotrexate as previously prescribed.
- Continue follow-up with his rheumatologist.

Numbness and tingling in the fingers and pain in the left wrist and hand.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
George is a patient with several months of pain and numbness in the left wrist and hand. It began on its own without a known cause. Symptoms are most noticeable at night. He sometimes wakes with the hand "asleep" and has to shake it out. Numbness involves all fingers but is more noticeable in the thumb and index finger, and at times the little finger is numb as well. He reports weakness in the left hand and drops things, mostly because he has difficulty feeling objects. He has no problems with the right hand so far. He works in landscaping, doing heavy labor with repetitive movements day in and day out. He drinks one to two beers on Fridays and Saturdays. No one has told him he has rheumatoid arthritis or any similar condition of the hand or wrist.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Musculoskeletal: Left wrist and hand pain and weakness. No right hand problems.
Neurologic: Numbness and tingling in the left hand and fingers, worse at night; dropping objects due to decreased sensation.
Other systems not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Cardiovascular and respiratory: Heart and lungs were briefly auscultated; no findings were stated.
Neurologic/Musculoskeletal: Grip strength is decreased on the left compared with the right. Light touch of the fingers is felt, but sensation feels abnormal on the thumb side more than the index finger side. Tinel's sign is positive bilaterally, with a jolt or zing into the fingertips on tapping both wrists.

RESULTS
No results available. EMG ordered (see plan).

- Follow up in the office in 2 weeks to determine whether further intervention is needed, including more diagnostic testing or possible surgical release of the pressure on the nerves.
- Patient agreed with the plan and had no further questions. The nurse will discharge him.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Right ankle pain after a fall.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Anna presents with right ankle pain after slipping on a patch of ice while taking out the trash last night. She heard a pop when she fell. She is concerned about a torn Achilles. Initially she was unable to bear weight and a friend helped her into the house. She can now put a little weight on it but is still limping. Pain was severe at onset and is now 6/10. It is constant and throbbing, and the ankle feels warm to the touch. She iced and elevated the ankle last night and took ibuprofen last night and this morning, with no real relief. She has never injured this ankle before. She played soccer in high school and had other injuries, but none to this ankle. She denies numbness and tingling. She has no prior history of ankle sprain.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Neurological: No numbness or tingling in the foot.
Musculoskeletal: Right ankle pain and difficulty walking, as per HPI.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Blood pressure 120/80. SpO2 98%. Heart rate was reviewed, but no value was stated.
Right ankle:
- Skin: Ecchymosis over the lateral malleolus with associated swelling. The ankle is slightly warm to palpation.
- Tenderness to palpation of the anterior lateral soft tissue.
- No laxity on anterior drawer or inversion stress testing.
- No bony tenderness on palpation of the foot.
Neurovascular, right foot: Capillary refill less than 3 seconds, strong dorsalis pedis pulse, sensation intact to light touch.

RESULTS
Right ankle x-ray: No fractures and no bony abnormalities.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Right ankle sprain, medium grade. Symptoms and exam are consistent with a sprain. X-ray shows no fracture.
- Keep the leg elevated when seated.
- Continue icing, about 5 times a day for 20 minutes at a time, to reduce swelling.
- Air cast provided to stabilize the ankle.
- Crutches provided. Stay off the leg for 1 to 2 days, then walk on it as tolerated.
- Expected course: able to walk on it in a day or two, soreness for a couple of weeks, and return to normal in about 2 to 3 weeks. Bruising should resolve.
- Work note requested and declined, as she works at a computer and can return to work.
- If pain continues or does not improve after this week, she should contact the office for re-evaluation and possible MRI.
- The patient had no further questions.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Yearly follow-up for asthma, allergic rhinitis, and food allergy.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Emily Hernandez is a 20-year-old female (DOB 03/26/2001) seen for yearly follow-up of asthma, allergic rhinitis, and food allergy. Written consent was obtained today to use DAX for documentation. Her last visit was a telemedicine visit in April 2020. Due to an insurance change, she was switched from Symbicort to Wixela.

Asthma: She currently uses Wixela 250/50, one puff, and reports it works well with no issues. She is trying to use it less because she hopes to enlist in the military in early spring 2022 (about 6-7 months away). She will need to perform fitness testing without an inhaler, and she wants to show her asthma is controlled without one. On average she takes it twice daily (one puff morning and one puff night) about 3-4 days per week and once daily (morning or night) on the other days. She feels this is working okay. She uses albuterol rarely, only before strenuous exertion such as a run, as prevention. She has no limitation with walking or errands. She wondered whether vocal cord dysfunction might play a role. She had no urgent care or ER visits for breathing in the past year and no prednisone courses. Over the past year she picked up vaping and smoking and is trying to quit; she now uses only a little. She has not used her nebulizer in a long time (last for bronchitis).

Allergic rhinitis: She uses Zyrtec (over the counter) mostly in spring and fall and as needed in summer. She does not take it daily but takes it on days she expects to be outside, including about 3 days per week when she works outside. It works great.

Food allergy: Known peanut allergy. Last year she developed hives after touching peanuts while cleaning a car at her job with Enterprise Rent-A-Car. Since then she wears long sleeves and changes gloves each time, and has had no further reactions. She carries an EpiPen. She previously had tree nut testing and recalls eating almonds without a reaction, but she tends to avoid all tree nuts.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Respiratory: No breathing problems requiring urgent care or ER visits; rare exertional albuterol use only as preventive.
Skin: No recent hives or reactions since the peanut contact exposure last year.
Allergic/Immunologic: Seasonal allergy symptoms well controlled with Zyrtec.
Other systems: Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Ears: Normal, with a small amount of wax bilaterally.
Mouth/throat: Normal on inspection.
Nose: Normal.
Lungs: Clear, sound terrific.
Heart: Normal on auscultation.

RESULTS
Spirometry today: About the same as results from a couple of years ago and slightly better. The 2019 test was done during wildfire smoke season, when values were slightly lower.
ACT score: 21.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Asthma: Well controlled with good spirometry. Patient has Kaiser insurance, which limits options. Options were discussed: continue Wixela off-label once daily, or step down to a single-medication inhaler, Alvesco. The patient chose to step down.
- Start Alvesco 80 mcg, two puffs twice daily, sent to Kaiser Permanente Broadway pharmacy.
- Keep Wixela aside, not discarded, in case Alvesco does not work well.
- Renew albuterol as needed.
- Possible future step-down to using inhaled steroid only when ill or during smoke season per newer guidelines, unless symptoms recur monthly.
- Repeat spirometry and ACT in 4 months; documentation may be needed for the military.
- No nebulizer refills needed.
- Encouraged to continue quitting smoking and vaping.

2. Allergic rhinitis: Zyrtec 10 mg as needed, over the counter.

3. Peanut allergy: Continue avoiding peanuts and tree nuts. EpiPen refilled.

Follow-up in 4 months with ACT and spirometry, sooner if needed. Visit time 25 minutes.

Numbness and tingling in both hands, referred for evaluation.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Mr. Cook is a 60-year-old right-handed male (DOB January 1, 1960; MRN abc123) referred for evaluation of numbness and tingling in both hands for a few weeks. He broke both wrists in a car accident last December. After the fractures healed, he noticed the tingling and numbness more. Both hands have worsened over the last month. The right is worse than the left, and his right wrist was in worse shape at the time of the fracture. He wears a splint on the right wrist and sometimes on the left, and the splint helps.

On the right, symptoms extend from the middle and ring fingers up the forearm. On the left, they involve the ring and pinky fingers. He describes the hands as mainly sore, sometimes throbbing, and feeling weaker, especially with use. Tingling is more prominent when the hands hurt, and is dull when the pain subsides. Symptoms are worse at night and come and go during the day. He denies loss of sensation, though the hands may be less sensitive than they should be. He has also had mild neck stiffness. He hit his head in the accident and was told it was a contusion. He was given nerve pain medication but has not been taking it as prescribed.

Medical history: hypertension (on Coreg), anxiety (on Lexapro), and prediabetes, controlled with diet. No history of thyroid issues.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: fatigue and weight gain.
Eyes: floaters.
Cardiovascular: shortness of breath and leg swelling.
GI: excessive appetite and bloating.
Endocrine: always hungry.
Skin: nail bed changes, dryness, itching.
Musculoskeletal: gout and muscle pain. Mild neck stiffness was also reported in the HPI.
Neurologic: numbness and tingling as above.
All other systems negative.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Neurologic:
- Sensation is normal except for diminished pin prick sensation in the third and fourth fingers on the right and decreased sensation in the fourth and fifth fingers on the left.
- Reflexes are 1+ and symmetric, with 2+ at the knees.
- Toes are downgoing bilaterally.
- Tinel sign is positive at both wrists and both elbows.
- The rest of the exam is normal.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, likely related to past trauma. Bilateral cubital tunnel syndrome is also possible, but the symptom presentation favors carpal tunnel syndrome.
- Order EMG/nerve conduction testing to pinpoint the site of nerve irritation.
- Continue wearing the splints.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Low back pain radiating down the left leg, referred by PCP.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Matthew is a patient referred by his PCP for low back pain. He reports the back pain has been present for a long time, but it became much worse about one month ago. He reports a fall off a roof approximately 30 years ago, after which he was told there may have been a fracture, and he was unable to play football. He points to the lower back as the site of pain, with radiation through the hip and down the left leg, along the side of the leg and calf to the big toe. He describes the pain as an "electrical toothache" that goes down the whole leg. Pain is 6/10 at the visit; he did not take his medications before the visit so the doctor could see him as he is. He states it reaches 13/10 at its worst. At one point he also rated the pain 8/10. Lying down is the only thing that relieves it. Standing, walking, sitting (including sitting in the waiting area for 30 minutes), coughing, and sneezing worsen it. He reports difficulty tying his shoes, that standing and going to the mall are very difficult, and that he has been essentially bedridden. He reports his foot drags when he walks and he has been using a cane. He reports weakness in his back and in both legs. He wonders whether he has spinal stenosis. He has previously tried NSAIDs without relief and has done physical therapy. He has heard from a friend that the doctor "burned some nerves" and is hoping for a procedure today.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Musculoskeletal: Positive for low back pain, left leg pain, back and bilateral leg weakness, and difficulty ambulating requiring a cane.
Neurological: Positive for radiating leg pain and foot drag. Numbness and tingling were asked about; the patient did not report them and described weakness instead.

Vitals: Look good per physician.
Back: No bony abnormalities, no redness, no bruising. Pain to palpation at the L4 vertebra. Pain with flexion and extension of the back.
Neuro/Extremities: Strength 4/5 in the left lower extremity and 5/5 on the right. Reflexes brisk. Motor and sensory intact in both lower extremities.

RESULTS
MRI: Disk herniation at L4-L5 with associated nerve root impingement (nerve compressed by the herniation).

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Acute disk herniation at L4-L5 with nerve root impingement, causing low back pain and left leg radicular pain. The patient is young and otherwise healthy and is expected to do well. NSAIDs and prior PT have not provided relief.
- Epidural steroid injection to be performed today with the patient's agreement, to place anti-inflammatory medication at the site of inflammation. The patient agreed. The nurse will prep him.
- Explained that the injection can take about 2 to 3 weeks to take full effect.
- Refer back to physical therapy for strengthening of the area.
- Follow up with the physician in about 1 month.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Vision changes, right eye.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Matthew is a patient who presents with vision changes. He reports difficulty adjusting to dark, dim environments, particularly when dining out at restaurants, and thinks he may have cataracts. Per the technician's notes, he also has decreased vision when reading, especially in dark places, and straight lines such as door frames appear crooked. Symptoms have been present for a while and have worsened over the last 3 to 4 months. He notes that the straight grooves in the paneling in his office look wavy.

He smokes about a pack per day. He has tried hypnosis, lozenges, and nicotine gum and gets close to quitting, but relapses when he goes out without his wife and buys cigarettes from others.

He has a history of high blood pressure. He has not taken his blood pressure medication for a while, as it is kept in a cupboard corner and he forgets it. It is not stated whether he checks his blood pressure regularly.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Eyes: Decreased vision in dim lighting and when reading, straight lines appearing wavy or crooked. Right eye is the concern.
Other systems: Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Eyes:
Anterior segment: Posterior chamber intraocular lenses in both eyes.
Right eye: Cornea clear. No NVI. Cup-to-disc ratio 0.2. Fundus exam shows retina attached 360 degrees with no holes or tears. RPE changes in the fovea. Posterior segment shows drusen in the macula, retinal thickening, subretinal fluid, and exudate accumulation. Positive for hemorrhage.
Left eye: Cornea clear. No NVI. Cup-to-disc ratio 0.3. RPE changes in the fovea. No hemorrhage and no subretinal fluid. Retina attached.

RESULTS
OCT: Drusen deposits under the RPE, subretinal fluid accumulation, and choroidal neovascular membrane visualized.
Fluorescein angiography: Focal area of leakage in the right eye, consistent with neovascular age-related macular degeneration.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Neovascular (wet) age-related macular degeneration, right eye. Exam and diagnostic testing are consistent with this diagnosis, at an advanced stage that usually leads to more severe vision loss. Abnormal blood vessels grow beneath the retina and leak fluid and blood, creating a central blind spot. The condition is the most common cause of severe vision loss.
- Monthly intravitreal Lucentis injections after the eye is numbed. The patient was told the injection should be painless with numbing.
- Injections may slow the rate of vision decline and possibly stop it, though some small vision loss may still occur. This is the best chance of maintaining vision.
- The patient had no questions. The nurse will prep him and the first injection will be given today.

2. Tobacco use, about 1 pack per day. Multiple prior quit attempts. Counseled on the importance of cutting back or quitting altogether.

3. Hypertension, nonadherent to medication. Counseled to take blood pressure medication as prescribed, starting today. Advised to place the pill bottle on the counter as a reminder.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Follow-up for adult hydrocephalus, first visit since shunt surgery on August 1, 2020.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Mr. Watson is an 86-year-old male (DOB 04/12/1934) who returns for follow-up of adult hydrocephalus. He has been followed since May 2020, when he first presented with eight to ten years of progressive gait impairment, cognitive impairment, and decreased bladder control. The diagnosis of adult hydrocephalus was established with a spinal catheter protocol in June 2020. He underwent shunt surgery on August 1, 2020, with placement of a Medtronic Strata programmable shunt in a ventriculoperitoneal configuration, programmed at level 2.0. He is accompanied by his daughter, Theresa.

He has not been sick or hospitalized since surgery, per his daughter. He has been doing much better.

Gait: Improved. He can now walk to the dining room, which he could not do before surgery. He still has times when he needs help.

Bladder: Improved somewhat after surgery but has since leveled off. He wears diapers. No skin sores from the diaper, and no decreased or painful urination.

Cognition: He feels better and no longer feels lost when talking with someone. His daughter relayed that his other daughter, Hannah, said she can have a normal conversation with him again.

He denies headaches, pain at the shunt site, and abdominal pain.

He asked whether he will be able to drive again.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Impaired ability to carry out daily functions. Negative for fever or unintentional weight loss.
GU: Urinary incontinence, wears a diaper. Negative for genital sores, decreased or painful urination.
Neurological: Continued walking impairment and cognitive impairment. Negative for headaches, recent falls, or hallucinations.
Psychiatric: Negative for depression, excessive worrying, or mood swings.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: BP 124/80, heart rate 64, respirations 18, weight 174 pounds, pain 0/10.
General: Pleasant and cooperative. Converses easily, though his daughter adds some details.
Shunt: Site clean, dry, and intact. Setting confirmed at 2.
Cranial nerves: Pupils equal. EOMs intact. Face symmetric. No dysarthria.
Motor: Normal bulk and strength. Coordination slow on finger to nose.
Cognitive testing: Tested for recent and remote memory, attention span, concentration, and fund of knowledge. MMSE 26/30 with spelling and 25/30 with calculations. He recalled two of three memory words with cuing and the third with multiple choice. Initial scores were 24/30 with spelling and 23/30 with calculations, and he could not recall any memory words with cuing and only one with multiple choice.
Gait: Tinetti assessment without an assistive device. Gait score 6 to 8 out of 12, balance score 12 out of 16, total 18 to 20 out of 28. Slightly improved from initial total of 15 to 17 out of 28.

RESULTS
CT head, 10/15/2020: Frontal horn span at the level of the foramen of Monro 4.6 cm. Third ventricular contour flat with a span of 10 mm. By the doctor's reading, there is a tiny amount of blood in the right frontal region with a tiny subdural collection, which was not noted by the radiologist, who reported no extra-axial fluid collections. Substantial small vessel ischemic change.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Adult hydrocephalus, status post VP shunt placement
2. Gait impairment
3. Urinary incontinence and urgency
4. Cognitive impairment

He has improved in gait, cognition, and to some extent bladder control since shunt surgery. The doctor does not believe the tiny fluid collection on CT is causing symptoms. He has no headaches or pain and has improved.

Plan:
- Leave the shunt setting unchanged for another two to three months.
- Return in three months. The appointment will be scheduled at the front desk.
- Driving: It is unlikely his movement speed will improve enough to pass a driver safety evaluation at this point. Some patients improve over nine to 12 months, and the doctor would be happy to recommend evaluation if he improves. He may enroll in a driver safety program in the meantime without a recommendation. Improvement will continue to be monitored.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Left shoulder pain for a few weeks.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Betty is a very active patient who reports left shoulder pain for approximately three weeks. She wonders whether it is bursitis. She cannot identify a specific inciting event but has been renovating her basement and doing a lot of work on it. She denies any trauma, falls, or hitting the shoulder. She has had occasional aches and pains in the past that were managed with Tylenol, but no prior pain in this shoulder is described as significant. The pain is isolated to the left shoulder.

She has significant pain when reaching for or lifting objects and does not attempt to raise her arm overhead because of pain. The pain is constant. It worsens with pressure, particularly when lying on the left side. She is a side sleeper and has difficulty sleeping because of this. The pain is present when lying on her back but increases when she lies directly on the shoulder.

She takes two extra-strength Tylenol every 6 to 8 hours, which takes the edge off. Pain is 7/10 without Tylenol and 2-3/10 with Tylenol. She denies numbness or tingling in the arm or hand.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Musculoskeletal: Left shoulder pain with limited use of the arm as above.
Neurological: No numbness or tingling in the arm or hand.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Reviewed by the physician; within normal limits.
Left shoulder: Limited active and passive range of motion. Tenderness over the greater tuberosity of the humerus. No tenderness at the sternoclavicular or clavicular joints.
Hand grip: Good bilaterally.
Neurovascular, left arm: Capillary refill brisk, less than 3 seconds. Motor and sensation intact to light touch.

RESULTS
X-ray of the left shoulder: No fracture or bony abnormality.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Left shoulder pain, most likely due to rotator cuff tendinopathy.
- Order MRI of the left shoulder to ensure no other pathology.
- Refer to physical therapy for approximately 6 to 8 weeks.
- Continue Tylenol as needed.
- If symptoms do not improve, consider a steroid injection of the left shoulder.
- Patient asked whether the pain will go away. The physician believes it will, noting many patients do well with PT, and will start with a conservative approach.
- Follow up in about 2 weeks. The nurse will provide paperwork.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Hypertension and palpitations. New patient visit for blood pressure that is not controlled on current medications.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Jordan Roberts is a 49-year-old man (DOB 3/2/1972) with hypertension and a history of palpitations. He was seen in the emergency room in March for high blood pressure and palpitations. That day he had a few cups of coffee and no breakfast. He thinks it was more likely a panic attack. The doctor wondered whether low blood sugar contributed. He has had no recurrence of the palpitations since.

He has had blood pressure problems since he was young. Many family members have high blood pressure. He thought his pressure was improving. About one month ago his new primary doctor started a combination medication, Benicar HCT 40-25 (contains hydrochlorothiazide). He also continues amlodipine 10 mg daily. He checks his blood pressure every morning on waking, and recent readings are about 146 to 155. He has not reached the 120s. He is trying to reduce his salt intake and feels he is doing well with it. He walks on the treadmill when he can.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Cardiovascular: Palpitations in March, none since.
Gastrointestinal: No abdominal tenderness on palpation.
Other systems not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Cardiovascular: Heart sounds good.
Respiratory: Lungs sound good.
Abdomen: Non-tender to palpation; the patient denied pain anywhere pressed.
Extremities: Ankles and feet examined with no swelling.

RESULTS
Potassium one week ago was 4.0. It has not been rechecked since.
The thyroid profile from March 1st, 2021 was requested to be copied forward. No values were discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Resistant hypertension. The patient is on three medications at maximum doses (amlodipine 10 mg, olmesartan, hydrochlorothiazide) and blood pressure remains above goal.
- Start spironolactone. The doctor discussed that it is effective for lowering aldosterone and blood pressure. Possible secondary drivers such as parathyroid abnormalities or aldosterone overproduction (hyperaldosteronism) were mentioned.
- Risks discussed: electrolyte disturbance, dehydration (dizziness on standing, so stay hydrated), hyperkalemia (rare; starting potassium of 4.0 leaves room), and low sodium when combined with hydrochlorothiazide. This does not mean he should eat more salt. Dizziness is possible. Gynecomastia occurs in about 1 in 100 men. If it occurs, he should stop the medication and notify the doctor. The patient voiced understanding.
- Metabolic panel and blood pressure check in 2 weeks, with follow-up in 2 weeks.
- If not controlled on spironolactone, refer to the resistant hypertension clinic to evaluate secondary causes and consider procedures such as renal denervation, which has been shown to lower blood pressure by about 10 points. Not everyone is a candidate.
- The next medication would be carvedilol, which the doctor tries to avoid because of the potential for erectile dysfunction. This was discussed with the patient.
- Counseling: DASH eating plan information provided. Keep salt under 2000 mg per day (recommendation is 1500 mg). Increase potassium. Exercise on the treadmill about 30 minutes most days, which could lower blood pressure by 7 to 10 points. Heart.org (American Heart Association) recommended for education.
- Discussed the importance of control to prevent cardiac enlargement, heart failure, kidney failure, and stroke.

2. Palpitations and prior ER visit. Likely related to caffeine, no breakfast, or a panic attack. No recurrence.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Left back pain from a suspected kidney stone. Follow-up of hypertension and diabetes.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Linda has a past medical history of hypertension and diabetes and a history of kidney stones. This is her third episode; she has not had one in a while. Pain began about 3 days ago in the left back and has since moved lower, now radiating toward the groin. The pain is constant, and she cannot get comfortable. She is able to urinate, but this morning she noticed blood in her urine. She reports chills and nausea, and she cannot eat because of the pain. She denies fever. She has taken Tylenol and ibuprofen without relief. She was previously advised to be cautious with ibuprofen because of her blood pressure. Previous stones took about 3-4 days to pass. She has not passed this stone yet. She suspects it might be a kidney infection.

Hypertension: She is on Norvasc 2.5 mg. She obtained a home blood pressure cuff but has not been consistent in using it. Systolic readings are usually in the 130s, sometimes in the 140s, and once reached 150. Diastolic readings are 70-80. At diagnosis her systolic pressure was in the 180s. She is trying to reduce salt intake to 2300 mg per day but admits difficulty, particularly with french fries. She is open to help with her diet.

Diabetes: She is on metformin 500 mg and takes it daily. Her last A1c was 7.3. She checks her fasting blood sugars daily, and they have been in the low 100s. A glucose of about 300 was noted a couple of months ago.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Positive for chills. Negative for fever.
Cardiovascular: Negative for chest pain.
Gastrointestinal: Positive for nausea and decreased appetite. Negative for abdominal pain.
Genitourinary: Positive for hematuria. Able to urinate.
Musculoskeletal: Positive for left back pain radiating toward the groin.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Cardiovascular: Grade 2/6 systolic ejection murmur, previously known.
Respiratory: Lungs clear bilaterally, no crackles or wheezes.
Abdomen: Tenderness to palpation, no rebound or guarding.
Back/Flank: CVA tenderness on the right flank per the doctor's exam. Back palpation is painful.
Vitals: Blood pressure was somewhat elevated at the visit, attributed to pain.

RESULTS
No results from today's visit. Previous A1c was 7.3. Glucose was about 300 on testing a couple of months ago.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Kidney stone, recurrent (third episode), with suspected inflammation around the kidney based on CVA tenderness.
- Prescribe oxycodone 5 mg every 6-8 hours as needed for pain.
- Continue Tylenol for breakthrough pain.
- Push fluids to help pass the stone.
- Provide a strainer to strain urine and check for the stone.
- Refer to urology, to be seen even if the stone passes, given recurrent stones and for prevention.

2. Hypertension.
- Continue Norvasc 2.5 mg with no changes.
- Continue home blood pressure monitoring at least three times a week.
- Limit salt intake to about 2300 mg per day.

3. Diabetes.
- Continue metformin 500 mg.
- Refer to a dietitian/nutrition for diet help. The goal is to potentially come off both medications in the future.

The patient understands and agrees with the plan.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Hospital follow-up after an acute on chronic congestive heart failure exacerbation.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is an 82-year-old male with a past medical history of hypertension and stage 3 chronic kidney disease. He presents for follow-up after a recent hospitalization for acute on chronic CHF exacerbation.

Before admission, he noticed ankle swelling despite trying to watch his diet. One day he became very short of breath and called 911. Paramedics placed him on a breathing mask. In the ER, his blood pressure was reported as very high (200/90 per the chart). He admits to sometimes missing a dose or two of his medications. He also admits to dietary indiscretion, particularly pizza and chicken wings at weekend parties with friends.

He was hospitalized for a couple of days. He received a medication that made him urinate a lot and IV diuretic. He believes his blood pressure medications were changed. He feels much better now. Since discharge he has been following his diet and taking his medications as instructed. He bought a home blood pressure cuff, which arrived last week. He checks it about every other day and reports his readings have been good.

He denies shortness of breath, difficulty with activity, trouble sleeping, and chest pain since returning home.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Feels well.
Cardiovascular: Positive for prior ankle swelling. Denies chest pain.
Respiratory: Denies shortness of breath currently.
Sleep: Denies trouble sleeping.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: BP 128/72, HR 79, RR 26 (doctor attributed to talking), O2 saturation 99%.
Neck: No jugular venous distention.
Cardiovascular: 2/6 systolic ejection murmur, previously heard and stable.
Respiratory: Lungs clear bilaterally.
Extremities: Trace lower extremity edema.

RESULTS
Echocardiogram: Preserved EF of 55%, abnormal diastolic filling, mild to moderate mitral regurgitation.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
82-year-old male with hypertension and stage 3 CKD, seen after hospitalization for acute on chronic CHF exacerbation.

1. Congestive heart failure, likely precipitated by dietary indiscretion and uncontrolled hypertension.
- Continue Bumex 2 mg daily.
- Continue to watch diet and avoid salty foods; cut back on pizza and chicken wings.
- Weigh daily and call if weight gain of about 3 pounds in 2 days.
- Refer to nutritionist for diet education.
- Continue monitoring the stable systolic murmur.

2. Hypertension. BP is well controlled today.
- Continue Cozaar 100 mg daily.
- Continue Norvasc 5 mg once daily.
- Order renal artery ultrasound to rule out secondary causes.
- Continue home BP monitoring.
- Take medications consistently.

3. Stage 3 chronic kidney disease.
- Obtain additional labs to ensure he tolerates the current regimen.

Follow-up in 3 months.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Uncontrolled hypertension. Referred by PCP for difficulty controlling blood pressure and abnormal kidney findings on recent blood work.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Virginia is a patient who started seeing a new PCP last year. Her PCP has adjusted her medications and added two blood pressure medications after noting elevated blood pressure. The patient reports she is now taking her medications consistently, though she was not adherent previously. Blood pressure remains difficult to control. Her PCP also noted something about her kidneys on her last blood work, and she was referred for further evaluation.

Most days she feels fine and remains busy at work, but she can tell when her blood pressure is high. She checks her blood pressure at home a few times a week with an electronic arm cuff. Readings have been trending higher, with a recent reading as high as 170/90. She called her PCP, who increased her medications again. She notes that CVS no longer has a blood pressure station since the pandemic.

Diet: She admits her diet could be better, especially during football season, when she eats a lot of pizza, wings, and subs. She is trying to cut down, particularly on non-game days.

Mild headaches occur only when blood pressure is very high. She denies chest pain and shortness of breath, including with exertion. She notices slight lower extremity swelling after being on her feet for a long time.

Current medications: amlodipine (Norvasc) 10 mg daily and carvedilol 25 mg twice daily. She was previously on lisinopril, which was changed with the adjustments. She takes NSAIDs (Advil, Motrin, Aleve) occasionally for knee or back pain, not daily.

Alcohol: A couple of beers during the week and one or two on the weekends.

Family history: Both parents have hypertension, and one had kidney disease.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Feels fine most days.
Cardiovascular: Denies chest pain. Mild swelling in lower extremities after prolonged standing.
Respiratory: Denies shortness of breath, including with exertion.
Neurological: Mild headaches only when blood pressure is very high.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: BP 169/74, heart rate 88, oxygen saturation 98%.
Neck: No jugular venous distention. No carotid bruits.
Lungs: Clear.
Cardiovascular: Grade 2/6 systolic ejection murmur.
Extremities: 1+ bilateral pitting edema.

RESULTS
No test results were reviewed. Per the patient, recent blood work done by her PCP raised a concern about her kidneys. No specific values were discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Uncontrolled hypertension. Etiology is likely multifactorial. Before further medication changes, testing will be done to look for a specific secondary cause.
- Renal artery ultrasound to evaluate for narrowing of the renal arteries.
- Morning aldosterone level, renin level, and 24-hour urine collection to evaluate for adrenal causes.
- Start doxazosin (Cardura) 4 mg once daily.
- Decrease alcohol to one or two drinks per week.
- Decrease salt intake significantly. Referral to a nutritionist.
- Stop NSAIDs (Advil, Motrin, Aleve). Use Tylenol only for pain.
- Record home blood pressures at the same time each day for the next 3 weeks and bring the log to the visit. She was informed that CVS on Main Street may have a blood pressure machine again.
- Follow up in 3 weeks.
- The doctor will communicate the plan to her PCP and remain in sync on treatment.

2. Systolic ejection murmur, grade 2/6, noted on exam. Will require a closer look. No specific workup was ordered during the visit.

3. Bilateral 1+ pitting edema. Noted on exam. No specific plan was discussed.

4. Kidney concern on recent bloodwork per PCP. Workup as above.

The patient voiced understanding and agreement with the plan.

He was previously referred to a dietitian but forgot whom he was supposed to see and needs a new order. He reports fasting glucose around 130. He thinks his last hemoglobin A1c was close to 16. He has a fondness for sweets, specifically chocolate chip cookies.

He has stage 3 chronic kidney disease. He had contrast dye exposure with the heart procedure. He last saw his nephrologist about a year ago. He has thrown out Motrin and Advil. He asked what he can take for headaches.

He reports feeling down since the heart attack and asks about medication for it. He denies thoughts of harming himself or others. He lives alone with his dog and finds it lonely. He is retiring and has plenty of time.

Neurologic: Dizziness when standing up quickly. Headaches (asks about pain medication for them).
Cardiovascular: No chest pain or exertional shortness of breath was reported. Leg swelling acknowledged ("I do have that").

- Continue aspirin for life. Continue Brilinta for another six months.
- Refill metoprolol, Crestor 40 mg once daily, and aspirin.
- Refer to cardiac rehab.

3. Diabetes, with elevated hemoglobin A1c.
- Order repeat hemoglobin A1c.
- Referral to dietitian for diabetic education.
- Doctor will discuss the insulin regimen with the primary care physician.

- Referral to psychiatry.

Medication refills will be sent to the patient's preferred pharmacy.
